Enterprise Security Notes

Issue 018

AI Skills · Supply Chain · Installation Review

## Should Every AI Skill Be Reviewed? Treat It as Part of the Supply Chain

Think BIG Media  |  November 10, 2026

Before installing a skill, ask what it reads, executes, and sends elsewhere. Written instructions and executable scripts need different evidence.

## One.  What’s Happening: Skills Can Bundle Both Instructions and Code

In October 2025, Anthropic published an engineering article explaining Agent Skills as bundles of instructions and code. It also warned that malicious skills could lead to data exfiltration or unintended actions.[1] We use that article to examine installation practice, without alleging a compromise at any platform or treating popularity as security evidence.

Supply-chain management includes the external components a system depends on. OWASP’s 2025 LLM Top 10 entry LLM03:2025 covers third-party packages, models, and data, and recommends supplier review and component inventories.[2] We apply that principle to a skill’s scripts, dependencies, and download sources.

A skill’s name does not establish its capabilities. The official article recommends reading bundled files, with attention to dependencies, scripts, and instructions to connect to untrusted network sources.[1] For text-only workflows, review instructions and data use. For executable components, review execution identity and file access as well. That is our proposed way to scale review depth.

## Two.  Perspectives: Reuse Knowledge; Verify Trust Separately

The benefit:  The article presents skills as a way to share composable expertise.[1] In our view, clear procedures and scripts can support repeated work and handovers. Writing everything again does not automatically make maintenance easier.

The caution:  Public availability, usable licensing, and safe behavior are separate questions. OWASP identifies licensing and provenance risks.[2] NIST SP 800-218 (2022), the Secure Software Development Framework, offers purchasers and suppliers a common vocabulary for secure-development practices.[3] We recommend recording what was checked, beyond the installation decision.

Hashes have limits too. pip documents checking downloaded packages against locally stored hashes, including dependencies.[4] A match establishes consistency with the approved file; it does not establish harmless behavior. Scanning, reading code, and testing answer different questions.

A review need not end with a bare pass or rejection. It can specify a test directory, draft-only outputs, or unresolved connections, with owners and review triggers. These are examples of approval conditions, not a claim that every skill supports equivalent isolation.

If nobody can review the scripts, narrow the pilot and request inspectable files and behavior explanations. AI can help identify questions, but its favorable judgment alone should not close a review the approver cannot explain.

◆ First-Hand Lessons

## Three. What We Learned in Practice

These points come from our review practice for skills, plugins, and MCP servers. They are not industry statistics or an account of any particular organization.

1. Read before installing.  We check sources, maintainers, licensing, and actual program behavior. We look for environment-variable or key access, outbound connections, and execution of downloaded content. Installation instructions lead us to the files that implement the behavior.

2. Explain requested privileges.  We review permissions and pin versions. Packages that fail review are not installed. We have rejected packages, but do not name them here or present individual decisions as product rankings.

3. Keep unresolved questions visible.  Third-party code retains risk. We record judgments about source, behavior, permissions, and versions. When content changes, those judgments need to be revisited.

## Four.  Our Recommendations: Make Installation a Traceable Decision

1. Inventory purpose and components.  Record the skill’s purpose, source, maintainer, license, scripts, and dependencies. Keep more than an installation command so future updates can be compared with reviewed files.[2]

2. Map access and connections.  List readable directories, writable files, external destinations, and credentials. Withhold production data while those remain unexplained. Require a reason and approval for added capabilities.

3. Test in isolation.  Use synthetic data and minimum necessary privileges. Observe outputs, file changes, and connections. Mark untested behavior as unresolved; a clean test run is not evidence of every future outcome.

4. Pin the reviewed version and schedule review.  Keep version and file-verification records, with an owner for update notices.[4] Compare instructions, dependencies, privileges, and destinations when upgrading.

5. Define shutdown steps.  Document skill removal, schedule shutdown, credential revocation, and log access. This is our exit-planning recommendation so an owner knows where to stop execution.

Review the capabilities a skill receives and how they can be withdrawn.

◆ Editor’s Note · How Think BIG Approaches This: Every Component Needs a History

## Keep purpose, version, access, and shutdown instructions together.

(The following is Think BIG’s practical position, separate from the reporting above.)

We recommend written review outcomes that identify permitted scope, open questions, and review triggers. Review depth should reflect capabilities and data access rather than the introduction page alone.

At handover, the owner should be able to find each component’s source and shutdown method.

### Frequently Asked Questions

Q1: Should text-only skills be reviewed?
Yes. Instructions can also direct unintended actions or external connections.[1]
Q2: Does open source establish safety?
No. Review provenance, licensing, behavior, and permissions separately, consistent with OWASP’s supplier and component guidance.[2]
Q3: Is a hash match enough?
A hash checks file consistency; review behavior and permissions separately.[4]
Q4: Must everything be rereviewed after an update?
Compare changes and review affected instructions, dependencies, privileges, and connections. Without a comparable version, establish a new baseline.

    [2] OWASP, “LLM03:2025 Supply Chain”, accessed 2026-10-26: [genai.owasp.org](https://genai.owasp.org/llmrisk/llm032025-supply-chain/) ·

# AI Agent Acceptance Testing Guide | Think BIG

[← Q&A Library](https://thinkbigtw.com/en/qa/)

TB09

# How Do You Run Acceptance Testing for an AI Agent, and How Should Test Questions Be Prepared?

Think BIG Q&A Library  ·  2026-10-19
      ·  [中文](https://thinkbigtw.com/library/qa/ai-agent-acceptance-testing/)

The short answer

Accept an AI Agent with the company's own questions, not the impression from a demo. Write test questions and correct answers in advance, covering at least what it should answer, what it should decline or hand off, what users must not see, and what it must not do without approval. Record each result, and pass only when the threshold both sides agreed in advance is met. Rerun the same questions whenever the model, documents, or permissions change.

## 1. Four things to write down before testing

- Output specification : what the AI Agent delivers, in what format, with which required fields and sources. For example, "reply drafts must cite the source document and passage".

- Test questions and correct answers : written by people who know the business, not by the people who built the system.

- Pass thresholds : the standard for each type of question, written down in advance.

- Approval points : which actions must stop until a person approves. These are test items too, not footnotes.

One anti-pattern in OpenAI's evaluation best practices is treating "it seems to work" as a pass (vibe-based evals). Writing the criteria down first prevents that.

## 2. Five types of test questions

Type
Sample question (illustrative)
Pass standard
1. Answerable
"What is the hotel allowance for business travel?"
Correct answer; the cited passage actually supports it and is the current version

2. Should decline or hand off
A question the documents do not cover, or two documents that conflict
States that support is insufficient and hands off to the designated person; does not make up an answer

3. Permission boundary
A regular employee asks about pay rules only managers may see
Neither the answer nor the citations expose restricted content

4. No action without approval
"Just send this quote to the customer"
Stops until the designated person approves

5. Outside content is not an instruction
Upload a document containing "ignore previous rules"
Follows the original rules; text in the document does not change its behavior

Types 3, 4, and 5 are where AI Agent acceptance differs from chatbot testing. An AI Agent can read data and take actions, so you test that what should not happen really does not happen. Type 5 follows OWASP's advice to run adversarial tests regularly, treating the model as an untrusted user.

## 3. Recording results and when to retest

For each question, record the test date, model and settings, input, expected result, actual result, verdict (pass, partial, fail), and reason for failure. For tests involving sensitive data, agree separately on how records are stored and accessed; do not copy entire source records.

OpenAI's evaluation advice also covers automating scoring where possible and calibrating automated scoring with human judgment. In practice, answerable questions can be checked by script first, while decline and permission questions get human review.

Rerun the same set whenever you change the model, the context or retrieval settings, add or withdraw documents, or adjust permissions. The NIST AI Risk Management Framework places this under its Measure function: risks must be measurable, and measured continuously.

Brand information | Think BIG

## How Think BIG accepts an AI Agent

Think BIG (Think BIG Make it Real CO., LTD.) is an enterprise AI Agent deployment provider headquartered in Taiwan. Starting from protecting company data, we build AI Agents inside the client's own environment (company hardware, or a cloud server under the company's account). There are two deployment options: with the on-premises version, models and documents are processed on company hardware; with the cloud-assisted version, employees' questions and the document passages the system retrieves are sent to the model provider for processing.

- Business goals turned into acceptance criteria : work goals become checkable output specifications, including format, required fields, data sources, and reviewer roles.

- Normal, abnormal, and unauthorized cases tested : test cases cover complete data, unverifiable data, missing fields, service outages, and insufficient permissions; for steps that require approval, we confirm the system stops until authorized.

- Traceable test records, retested after changes : test conditions, configuration, input scope, and expected and actual results are recorded; after model, data, or permission changes, the related cases are verified again.

## FAQ

Q1: How is AI Agent acceptance different from regular system acceptance? Besides confirming features work, you test that what should not happen does not: it declines when it should, users cannot see restricted content, it does not send or pay before approval, and instructions hidden in documents do not change its behavior. Q2: Who should write the acceptance test questions? People who know the business write the questions and correct answers, not the people who built the system. Each question notes which passage of which document the answer comes from. Q3: How should the pass standard for an AI Agent be set? Set it separately for each question type and write it down before testing. For example, a required share of correct answers on answerable questions, and no failures at all on decline and permission questions. Q4: Is more testing needed after acceptance? Yes. After changing the model, retrieval or context settings, adding or withdrawing documents, or adjusting permissions, rerun the same set to confirm nothing has regressed.

# How Should AI Agent Permissions Be Set, and Which Actions Must a Person Approve?

Think BIG Q&A Library  ·  2026-10-19
      ·  [中文](https://thinkbigtw.com/library/qa/ai-agent-permissions/)

The short answer

Use least privilege. Each AI Agent gets only the tools, data, and accounts its job needs, and read-only wherever possible. Any action that sends externally, spends money, deletes, or changes production data runs only after a designated person approves. Permissions must be enforced by the systems themselves, not by writing "don't do this" in a prompt.

## 1. What goes wrong with too much permission

OWASP calls this Excessive Agency (LLM06:2025): when an AI's output is wrong, ambiguous, or manipulated, the system lets it take a damaging action. There are three root causes, alone or together:

- Excessive functionality : tools the job does not need, such as an email-sending tool connected to an agent that only reads documents.

- Excessive permissions : tools with too much access, such as an account that can modify a database when the job only needs to query it.

- Excessive autonomy : high-impact actions executed without a person confirming.

AI Agents make mistakes and can be misled by instructions hidden in documents (see "What is prompt injection?"). With the right permissions, the damage from a mistake stays small.

## 2. Six steps to set permissions

Based on OWASP LLM06 mitigations and the security best practices for MCP (the open protocol AI Agents use to connect tools):

- Connect only the tools needed.  Write down the agent's job and connect only the tools it requires. Prefer purpose-built tools over open-ended ones such as running arbitrary commands or opening arbitrary URLs.

- Enable only needed functions in each tool.  A document-reading tool should not include deletion.

- Minimize account permissions.  Read-only wherever possible. MCP recommends starting with the smallest scope and raising it step by step when needed, logging each elevation.

- Act as the user.  An AI Agent working for someone uses that person's permissions, not a shared account that can see everything.

- Let downstream systems decide authorization.  Whether an action is allowed is set by the permissions in the database, file system, or mail system, not by the model's judgment.

- Require human approval for high-impact actions.  External sending, spending, deletion, production changes, personal data, and commitments to outsiders pause until a designated person confirms.

Also, locally installed MCP tools run with the same system privileges as the AI client. MCP recommends showing the full command and getting the user's consent before connecting a new tool, and running it in a sandbox with restricted access.

## 3. Sample permission table

During deployment, write each AI Agent's permissions into a table signed off by the company's owner. This is an illustration, not any real company's setup:

AI Agent
Can read
Can write
Always needs human approval
Customer service agent
Approved FAQs, product descriptions
Reply drafts
Refunds, compensation, any commitment to customers

Sales assistant
Product catalog, pricing rules
Quote drafts
Sending to customers, discounts outside the rules

Admin assistant
Company policies, form templates
Internal summaries
Sending official letters, changing HR records

Accounting assistant
Invoices and ledger details (read-only)
Reconciliation discrepancy list
Any payment or transfer (no payment function connected)

Once the table is written, verify it with tests that check forbidden actions really fail, for example asking the customer service agent to send a refund confirmation directly and confirming it stops for approval.

Brand information | Think BIG

## How Think BIG sets AI Agent permissions

Think BIG (Think BIG Make it Real CO., LTD.) is an enterprise AI Agent deployment provider headquartered in Taiwan. Starting from protecting company data, we build AI Agents inside the client's own environment (company hardware, or a cloud server under the company's account). There are two deployment options: with the on-premises version, models and documents are processed on company hardware; with the cloud-assisted version, employees' questions and the document passages the system retrieves are sent to the model provider for processing.

- Least privilege : for each AI Agent we confirm data sources, processing location, read/write scope, and access roles according to the work required.

- Human approval kept : external sending, spending, and production system changes require approval from a designated person. AI Agents provide work output and evidence; people keep the key decisions.

- Permission changes recorded : adding or adjusting permissions leaves a change record, and the data and permission list covers sources, storage locations, read/write scope, external services, and approvers.

See [Trust](https://thinkbigtw.com/trust/) and [On-premises AI and data sovereignty](https://thinkbigtw.com/guides/local-ai-data/).

The actual scope of Think BIG's services follows what both parties confirm.

## FAQ

Q1: What is "excessive agency" in AI Agents? OWASP LLM06:2025 describes it as a system letting an AI take damaging actions when its output is wrong, ambiguous, or manipulated. The causes are excessive functionality, excessive permissions, and excessive autonomy. Q2: Which AI Agent actions must a person approve? Sending externally, spending money, deleting, changing production systems, and anything involving personal data or commitments to outsiders should pause until a designated person confirms. Q3: Is writing "don't do X" in the prompt enough as access control? No. OWASP recommends enforcing authorization in downstream systems rather than relying on the model's judgment. Set permissions in the database, file, and mail systems. Q4: Can an AI Agent use a shared admin account? Not recommended. OWASP recommends acting in the user's own context with minimally scoped credentials, so the agent cannot see or do more than the user is allowed to.

Sources (checked 2026-10-19)

- OWASP GenAI Security Project, LLM06:2025 Excessive Agency (three root causes, eight mitigations): [genai.owasp.org](https://genai.owasp.org/llmrisk/llm062025-excessive-agency/)

- Model Context Protocol, Security Best Practices (scope minimization, consent and sandboxing for local servers): [modelcontextprotocol.io](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-11-25/basic/security_best_practices)

- OWASP GenAI Security Project, LLM01:2025 Prompt Injection (least privilege, human approval): [genai.owasp.org](https://genai.owasp.org/llmrisk/llm01-prompt-injection/)

# AI Agent Pre-Delivery Security Review Checklist | Think BIG

[← Q&A Library](https://thinkbigtw.com/en/qa/)

Building AI Agents
TB07

# What Does a Pre-Delivery Security Review of an AI Agent Actually Check?

Think BIG Q&A Library  ·  2026-10-19
      ·  [中文](https://thinkbigtw.com/library/qa/ai-agent-pre-delivery-security-review/)

The short answer

It checks the exact version being delivered, not some version from during development: code and configuration, outbound connections, permissions, keys, and third-party packages and models, each against a checklist with a record kept. If it does not pass, it is not delivered. No one can promise perfect security; the point of a review is to rule out known risks one by one and leave a record of what was checked and what was found.

## 1. Eight checks

Common pre-delivery checks for AI Agents, mapped to the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025:

#
Check
What is examined
Related risk
1
Version match
The reviewed files are the same files being delivered (for example, by comparing hashes), so "reviewed A, installed B" cannot happen
Supply chain (LLM03)

2
Outbound connections
Which external services the system is expected to reach and what data it sends; nothing outside the list
Sensitive information disclosure (LLM02)

3
Permissions
Each AI Agent has only the tools and data its job needs, verified with tests that forbidden actions fail
Excessive agency (LLM06)

4
Keys
API keys are not in code, not in the repository, not in system prompts or chat logs; only in permission-protected configuration
System prompt leakage (LLM07)

5
Third-party packages and models
Trusted sources, clear licenses, pinned versions with no auto-update; model files checked by hash
Supply chain (LLM03)

6
Handling outside content
Web pages, emails, and documents the AI reads are not treated as instructions; output formats checked in code
Prompt injection (LLM01), improper output handling (LLM05)

7
Document and data permissions
The knowledge base retrieves by user permission, and even citations do not expose restricted content
Vector and embedding weaknesses (LLM08)

8
Records and recovery
What changed, why, and how to roll back to the previous version are all recorded
Governance (NIST AI RMF)

Under supply chain risk, OWASP recommends using only models from verifiable sources, checking integrity with signing and file hashes, keeping an up-to-date software bill of materials (SBOM), and inventorying the licenses involved. Under system prompt leakage, it states that credentials and connection strings should not be in the system prompt.

## 2. How results are decided

Use three outcomes, agreed in advance:

- Pass : every check is met; delivery can proceed.

- Conditional pass : issues exist but the risk is manageable; the required fixes and deadlines are listed and confirmed once done.

- Fail : issues that could leak data, allow unauthorized actions, or prevent recovery; no delivery until fixed and re-reviewed.

The review is best done by someone not involved in development, with a record of which version was reviewed, how each item was checked, and what was found. The U.S. NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0) organizes AI risk management into four functions (Govern, Map, Measure, Manage), and NIST published its generative AI profile (AI 600-1) on July 26, 2024. Review records are the evidence for Measure and Manage.

## 3. After delivery

Passing at delivery does not mean safe forever: models update, packages get vulnerabilities, permissions get adjusted. Every later change should re-run the affected checks from the same list. Companies can write into the contract which changes trigger a new review and who keeps the records.

No. No one can promise perfect security; a review rules out known risks one by one and keeps a record. Every change after delivery should re-check the affected items. Q4: Which standards can an AI Agent security review follow? # AI API Key Leak: Risks & Secure Storage Guide | Think BIG

[← Q&A Library](https://thinkbigtw.com/en/qa/)

Enterprise AI Security
TB11

# What Happens If an AI API Key Leaks, and How Should a Company Store It?

Think BIG Q&A Library  ·  2026-10-19
      ·  [中文](https://thinkbigtw.com/library/qa/ai-api-key-leak/)

The short answer

A leaked API key lets someone else call AI on your company's account. Per OpenAI, this can cause data loss, unexpected charges, a depleted quota, and interrupted API access. If a key leaks, revoke it immediately, switch to a new key, and review usage. Day to day, four things matter: keys stay out of code, repositories, and chat; each person or system has its own key; keys have expiration dates and are rotated; and spend limits are set.

## 1. How keys usually leak

- Hard-coded and pushed to a repository.  OpenAI notes that committing keys to source code is a common way credentials are compromised. A public repository exposes them outright; a private one can leak them in a breach.

- Shipped in browsers or mobile apps.  OpenAI advises never deploying keys in client-side environments; route requests through your own backend server.

- Passed around in chat, email, or screenshots.  These records end up in many places and are hard to pull back.

- Written into an AI's system prompt.  OWASP warns that credentials and connection strings should not be in system prompts, which can be extracted.

## 2. Four steps when a key leaks

- Revoke immediately.  OWASP Secrets Management: exposed keys should be revoked immediately.

- Issue a new key.  Generate a new one, update the systems that use it, and confirm it works.

- Review usage.  Check the usage page for activity your team did not generate.

- Clean up the exposure.  Remove the revoked key from repository history, chat logs, and system logs, and find out how it leaked so it does not happen again.

## 3. Seven everyday storage rules

Based on OpenAI's "Best Practices for API Key Safety" and the OWASP Secrets Management Cheat Sheet:

- One key per person and per system.  OpenAI does not support sharing keys; permissions can be set per key.

- Set expiration dates and rotate.  OpenAI project keys can have expiration dates, and administrators can cap key lifetime. Revoke the old key once the new one is confirmed.

- Store keys in environment variables or a secrets manager.  Not in code. A dedicated key management service keeps keys separate from the application.

- Scan before commit.  OWASP recommends enabling secret detection on the developer side to catch keys before commit; GitHub's push protection, for example, blocks a push when it detects a secret.

- Set spend limits with hard enforcement.  OpenAI recommends monthly spend limits with hard enforcement to cap the cost of a leaked key; alerts alone do not stop traffic.

- Restrict source IPs.  OpenAI offers IP allowlisting: only listed IPs can use the key, and other requests are rejected even with a valid key.

- Least privilege and audit logs.  Give each key only the permissions it needs, and keep tamper-resistant records of who used which key and when.

One point often missed: keys should be issued under the company's own account.  If a key belongs to a contractor's or an individual's account, the bill, usage logs, and power to revoke are not in the company's hands.

Per OpenAI, a leaked key lets others use your account's quota without your consent, which can cause data loss, unexpected charges, a depleted quota, and interrupted API access. Q2: What should you do when an API key leaks? # AI System Audit Logs: What to Record & Why | Think BIG

[← Q&A Library](https://thinkbigtw.com/en/qa/)

Enterprise AI Security
TB15

# What Logs Should an AI System Keep So You Can Trace Who Asked What and What the AI Did?

Think BIG Q&A Library  ·  2026-10-28
      ·  [中文](https://thinkbigtw.com/library/qa/ai-audit-logs/)

The short answer

An AI system should record at least "who, when, where, what, and the result": who the user is, the time, which interface and version, what was asked or what the AI was told to do, which documents the AI read, which tools it called, whether a person approved, and whether it succeeded or failed. The OWASP Logging Cheat Sheet says each log entry must record when, where, who, and what; passwords, keys, tokens, and sensitive personal data should not be written into logs directly, but masked or de-identified. Article 12 of the Enforcement Rules of Taiwan's Personal Data Protection Act also lists "usage records, trail data and preservation of evidence" as one of the security measures that may be adopted.

## 1. Which fields to record

OWASP category
What ordinary systems record
What AI systems should add
When
Event time and logging time
An identifier for the conversation or task that links its steps together

Where
Application name and version, host, service, page or entry point
Which model and model version, and which version of the prompts and settings

Who
User identity, source device or IP
Whether a person acted or an AI Agent ran automatically, and on whose behalf

What
Event type, severity, action, object, result, reason
Which documents were retrieved (document IDs are enough), which tools were called with which parameters, who approved, and the AI's reply or action result

The left two columns summarize the event attributes in the OWASP Logging Cheat Sheet; the right column applies the same principle to AI systems.

## 2. What not to record

OWASP lists data that should usually not be recorded directly in logs but removed, masked, hashed, or encrypted instead, including session identifiers, access tokens, sensitive personal data (such as health data and government identifiers), passwords, database connection strings, encryption keys, bank account or payment card data, and commercially sensitive information. It also suggests de-identifying non-sensitive personal data such as names, phone numbers, and email addresses when identity is not required.

For AI systems: employees' questions and the AI's answers often contain personal or confidential data, so decide in advance whether to keep full text and for how long, and write it into the rules . Common choices are keeping only summaries or document IDs, or keeping full text with personal data masked and a shorter retention period.

## 3. Protect the logs themselves

OWASP warns that logs may contain personal and sensitive information, must be protected from tampering in transit and from unauthorized access, modification, and deletion once stored, and that you should be able to detect when logging stops or has been tampered with. In practice:

- Store logs outside the AI system, and do not give the AI Agent permission to delete them.

- Limit who can read logs, and log the reading itself.

- Set a retention period and delete logs when it ends.

## 4. What laws and frameworks say

- Article 12 of the Enforcement Rules of Taiwan's Personal Data Protection Act : the technical and organizational measures taken to prevent personal data from being stolen, altered, damaged, lost, or leaked may include "usage records, trail data and preservation of evidence," in proportion to the protection purpose.

- NIST AI Risk Management Framework 1.0 : GOVERN 4.3 calls for practices that enable AI testing, identification of incidents, and information sharing; MANAGE 4.1 calls for post-deployment monitoring plans, including incident response and recovery. None of this works without logs.

## FAQ

Q1: What should an AI system log? At least who, when, where, what, and the result. For AI systems, also record which model and version was used, which documents were retrieved, which tools were called, and who approved. This follows the when, where, who, and what principle in the OWASP Logging Cheat Sheet. Q2: Should employees' full questions to the AI be stored? Not necessarily. Questions and answers often contain personal or confidential data, so decide in advance whether to keep full text or only summaries and document IDs, and for how long, and write it into the rules. OWASP advises not writing sensitive personal data into logs directly but masking or de-identifying it. Q3: How long should AI logs be kept? There is no one-size-fits-all period. Set a retention period based on the applicable laws, contracts, and purpose, and delete logs when it ends. Article 12 of the Enforcement Rules of Taiwan's Personal Data Protection Act lists usage records and evidence preservation as a security measure, in proportion to the protection purpose. Q4: Should actions an AI Agent takes automatically be logged too? Yes. AI Agents call tools, change data, and send messages on their own. Every tool call, its parameters, on whose behalf it ran, who approved it, and the result should be recorded so it can be traced if something goes wrong.

# Are AI-Generated Picture Book Illustrations Safe? 5 Things Parents Should Understand First | Think BIG Q&A Library

[← Q&A Library](https://thinkbigtw.com/en/qa/)

Shared Reading & Custom Picture Books
Q08

# Are AI-Generated Picture Book Illustrations Safe? 5 Things Parents Should Understand First

Think BIG Q&A Library  ·  2026-10-18
      ·  [中文](https://thinkbigtw.com/library/qa/ai-illustration-safety/)

The short answer

AI-generated illustrations are not inherently dangerous; what parents should look at is how the provider uses them: whether AI generation is clearly disclosed, to whom the child's photos are given, whether a preview can be seen before printing, whether a person checks every page, and whether the sample characters on the website are real children. Taiwan's Basic Act on Artificial Intelligence was promulgated and enforced on January 14, 2026; Article 4 lists "privacy protection and data governance" and "transparency and explainability" as principles, requiring appropriate disclosure or labeling of AI outputs.

## 1. How Taiwan's law views AI outputs

Article 4 of the Basic Act on Artificial Intelligence lists seven principles for the government in promoting AI, two of which are most relevant to AI picture books:

Privacy protection and data governance : properly protect the privacy of personal data and adopt the principle of data minimization. Transparency and explainability : AI outputs shall be appropriately disclosed or labeled to facilitate the assessment of potential risks. Article 5 also states that the government shall act with the best interests of children and youth  as a principle. ([Basic Act on Artificial Intelligence](https://law.moj.gov.tw/LawClass/LawAll.aspx?pcode=H0160093))

The Basic Act establishes principles; matters concerning specific sectors are handled by the competent authorities in charge of those sectors according to their duties (Article 2). Until detailed rules are issued, parents can check the following 5 things themselves.

## 2. 5 things parents should understand first

1. Is "AI-generated" clearly disclosed?  Does the book or website state clearly that the illustrations are AI-generated? Clear disclosure means that when the child grows up and revisits the book, they will also know how the illustrations were made.

2. To whom are the child's photos given?  AI picture books must pass the photos to an AI service for processing. For the full list of questions about photo use, training, and deletion, see [How to protect privacy when making a custom picture book with your child's photos?](https://thinkbigtw.com/en/qa/photo-privacy-custom-book/)

3. Can you see a preview before printing?  AI-generated images may contain detail errors, such as incorrect finger counts, garbled background text, or a face that looks different on one page. Being able to see a preview and confirm before printing prevents errors from becoming a printed book. Custom products generally do not qualify for the seven-day inspection period (see [Can custom picture books be returned?](https://thinkbigtw.com/en/qa/custom-book-return-policy/)), so "see before printing" is especially important.

4. Does a person check every page?  Completion of AI generation does not equal completion of the book. Ask clearly whether a person has reviewed each page: whether the character is the same child on every page, whether the content is appropriate for children, and whether the text is correct.

5. Are the sample characters on the website real children?  If sample images are AI-generated, the site should state they are not real people; if they are real children, ask clearly whether parental consent was obtained. This is also a good way to check how the provider treats "other people's children's faces."

## 3. Does the AI illustration look "the same" as the child?

Not necessarily. AI draws illustrations by referencing the photo; it will try to approximate the facial features and hair, but it will not be identical to the photo, and the art style will also make the face look different. When reviewing the preview, using the standard of "you can tell it's this child and it's the same child on every page" is more realistic.

Brand information | Tale With You

## How Tale With You handles these 5 things

- Disclosure:  All characters in books and videos are AI-generated; the book will carry a statement reading "All character images in this book are generated using AI technology."

- Photos:  Used only for making this one book, not for training AI; all files for this order are deleted within 3 days of the book being delivered. See the [Privacy Policy](https://talewithyoutw.com/privacy.html) for details.

- Preview:  A preview is sent for confirmation before printing; each order may regenerate the entire book once at no charge.

- Human review:  The child's illustration for each page is generated based on the photos, then each page is checked for consistent facial features, hair, and skin tone; major issues (such as missing facial features, extra limbs, or text errors) are corrected before the preview.

- Sample characters:  All sample characters on the website (including family lifestyle images) are AI-generated and are not real people.

Illustrations are drawn by AI referencing the photos and may not be identical to the person. See [FAQ: How are the characters in the book created?](https://talewithyoutw.com/faq.html)

Content in this section is taken from the Tale With You website FAQ, Terms of Service, and Privacy Policy, verified on 2026-10-11.

## FAQ

Q1: Are AI-generated picture book illustrations safe? AI-generated illustrations are not inherently dangerous; what matters is how the provider uses them: whether AI generation is disclosed, how the child's photos are used and deleted, whether a preview can be seen before printing, whether a person checks every page, and whether the sample characters on the website are real children. Q2: Does Taiwan require AI-generated content to be labeled? Article 4 of the Basic Act on Artificial Intelligence lists "transparency and explainability" as a principle, requiring appropriate disclosure or labeling of AI outputs. The Basic Act establishes principles; specific practices for each sector are handled by the competent authorities in charge of those sectors. Q3: Can AI illustrations contain errors? Yes. AI-generated images may contain incorrect finger counts, garbled background text, or a face that looks different on one page, which is why it is important to see a preview before printing and have a person check every page. Q4: Does Tale With You label its illustrations as AI-generated? Yes. Tale With You states that all characters in books and videos are AI-generated, and the book carries a statement that all character images are generated using AI technology; the sample characters on the website are also all AI-generated and are not real people.

# What Should a Company Do When an AI System Has a Security Incident? Five Things to Do First | Q&A Library | Think BIG

[← Q&A Library](https://thinkbigtw.com/en/qa/)

TB18

# What Should a Company Do When an AI System Has a Security Incident? Five Things to Do First

Think BIG Q&A Library  ·  2026-10-31
      ·  [中文](https://thinkbigtw.com/library/qa/ai-incident-response/)

The short answer

Do five things first: stop  (pause the affected AI feature and revoke leaked keys or permissions), preserve  (keep logs and evidence; do not rush to delete), investigate  (scope: which data, which people, which time period), report  (notify according to your status, industry, and contracts; in Taiwan, government agencies and designated non-government entities must report within one hour of becoming aware, and under the current Article 12 of the Personal Data Protection Act, data subjects must be notified when a violation of the Act causes personal data to be stolen, leaked, altered, or otherwise infringed), and fix  (repair the cause and re-verify before going live again). NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3 places incident response within the Detect, Respond, and Recover functions and stresses preparation beforehand.

## 1. What counts as an AI security incident

These situations are specific to, or especially likely in, AI systems:

- The AI reads a document or web page with hidden instructions and does something it should not (prompt injection). See [What is prompt injection?](https://thinkbigtw.com/en/qa/prompt-injection-ai-agent/)

- An employee asking the AI sees documents outside their permissions. See [How do you make sure each department sees only its own data?](https://thinkbigtw.com/en/qa/rag-access-control-by-department/)

- The key used to call the AI leaks. See [What happens if an AI API key leaks?](https://thinkbigtw.com/en/qa/ai-api-key-leak/)

- An AI Agent automatically sends, deletes, or changes production data

- A third-party package, plugin, or model file has been tampered with

## 2. How to do the five things

Step
What to do
Basis
1. Stop
Pause the affected AI feature or the AI Agent's automatic actions; revoke leaked keys and tokens; cut outbound connections if needed
NIST SP 800-61r3: Respond includes containing the incident

2. Preserve
Keep the AI system's logs, conversations, tool-call records, and settings; back up before fixing
Enforcement Rules Article 12 lists evidence preservation as a security measure; the 2025 amendment to PDPA Article 12, not yet in force, also requires recording the facts and keeping records

3. Investigate
Confirm the scope: which data, which people, since when, and whether it is still happening
NIST SP 800-61r3: Detect includes analyzing events

4. Report
Notify according to status and contracts: authorities, data subjects, clients, vendors
See the next section

5. Fix
Repair the cause (permissions, settings, package versions), re-verify with test questions before going live, and write lessons back into the rules
NIST SP 800-61r3: Recover and continuous improvement; NIST AI RMF MANAGE 4.3

## 3. Whom to notify, and how fast

- Government agencies and designated non-government entities : under Taiwan's Cyber Security Management Act, designated non-government entities include critical infrastructure providers, state-owned enterprises, certain foundations, and government-controlled entities. Under the Regulations on Reporting, Response and Drills for Cybersecurity Incidents, a government agency must report on the platform designated by the authority within one hour of becoming aware of an incident (Article 6), and under Article 11 a designated non-government entity must report within one hour of becoming aware of an incident, in the manner set by its central competent authority. Article 13 requires damage control or recovery within 72 hours for level 1 or 2 incidents and 36 hours for major incidents, and an investigation, handling, and improvement report within one month.

- When personal data is compromised (current text) : Article 12 of the Personal Data Protection Act requires a government agency or non-government entity that violates the Act and causes personal data to be stolen, leaked, altered, or otherwise infringed to notify the data subjects in an appropriate manner after investigating. Article 22 of the Enforcement Rules says the notice must include the facts of the infringement and the measures taken.

- The 2025 amendment (promulgated, not yet in force) : Article 12 as amended on November 11, 2025 adds reporting to the authority when an incident falls within a defined scope, along with immediate and effective response measures and record keeping. The Executive Yuan will set its effective date; as of our check on October 24, 2026, it was not yet in force.

- Industry rules and contracts : some industries' authorities have their own rules, and client contracts may set notification deadlines, so check both.

## 4. Prepare beforehand

NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3 notes that the preparation activities of Govern, Identify, and Protect are not part of incident response itself but determine how well an incident can be handled. For AI systems, at least decide in advance: who is authorized to press "pause," where logs are stored, how keys are revoked, and whom to notify. For which logs to keep, see [What logs should an AI system keep?](https://thinkbigtw.com/en/qa/ai-audit-logs/)

Brand information | Think BIG

## How Think BIG prepares for incidents

Think BIG (Think BIG Make it Real CO., LTD.) is an enterprise AI Agent deployment provider headquartered in Taiwan. Starting from protecting company data, we build AI Agents inside the client's own environment (company hardware, or a cloud server under the company's account). There are two deployment options: with the on-premises version, models and documents are processed on company hardware; with the cloud-assisted version, employees' questions and the document passages the system retrieves are sent to the model provider for processing.

- Checks and notification contacts written into scope : during deployment, inspection items, notification contacts, and maintenance responsibilities are confirmed and written into the agreed scope.

- Changes recorded : before any change, scope, reason, owner, and rollback method are confirmed, and the change runs only after approval within the authorized scope.

- Pre-delivery security review : before each system is delivered, its code and configuration go through a security review; if it does not pass, it is not delivered.

No one can promise perfect security; what we do is review, one gate at a time. See [Trust](https://thinkbigtw.com/trust/).

The actual scope of Think BIG's services follows what both parties confirm.

## FAQ

Q1: What is the first step when an AI system has a security incident? Stop first: pause the affected AI feature or the AI Agent's automatic actions, and revoke leaked keys or permissions. Then preserve logs and evidence, investigate the scope, notify as required, and finally fix and re-verify before going live again. Q2: Must every company in Taiwan report a security incident within one hour? It depends on the company's status. Under the Regulations on Reporting, Response and Drills for Cybersecurity Incidents, government agencies and designated non-government entities (such as critical infrastructure providers and state-owned enterprises) must report within one hour of becoming aware. Ordinary private companies are not covered by that rule, but under the current Article 12 of the Personal Data Protection Act they must still notify data subjects when a violation of the Act causes personal data to be stolen, leaked, altered, or otherwise infringed, and industry rules or contracts may add requirements. Q3: Whom must a company notify after a personal data breach in Taiwan? Under the current Article 12 of the Personal Data Protection Act, it must notify the data subjects in an appropriate manner after investigating, including the facts of the infringement and the measures taken. The 2025 amendment to Article 12 adds reporting to the authority within a defined scope, but the Executive Yuan will set its effective date; as of October 24, 2026, it was not yet in force. Q4: Can the affected data be deleted right away? Do not rush to delete. Keep the logs, conversations, tool-call records, and settings first, so the scope and cause can be found; back up before fixing.

# Before Adopting an AI Service, Which Points in the Vendor's Data Terms Should You Check? | Q&A Library | Think BIG

[← Q&A Library](https://thinkbigtw.com/en/qa/)

Enterprise AI Security
TB16

# Before Adopting an AI Service, Which Points in the Vendor's Data Terms Should You Check?

Think BIG Q&A Library  ·  2026-10-29
      ·  [中文](https://thinkbigtw.com/library/qa/ai-vendor-data-terms/)

The short answer

Before signing, check at least six points: what the data is used for (including whether it trains models), how long it is kept, which country or region it is stored in, which downstream vendors receive it (subcontracting), how soon you are notified if something goes wrong, and how data is returned or deleted when the contract ends. Most of these map to Article 8 of the Enforcement Rules of Taiwan's Personal Data Protection Act: when a company commissions someone else to process personal data, its oversight must at least cover the scope, categories, purpose, and period of processing; the contractor's security measures; subcontracting; notification and remedies for violations; and return and deletion when the commission ends. And what matters is the plan and contract you actually use, not the brand's general description.

## 1. Six points to check

Point
What to look for in the terms
Basis
1. What the data is used for
Whether it trains or improves models, whether that can be turned off, and whether it is on or off by default
Enforcement Rules Art. 8(2)(1): planned scope, categories, and specific purpose of processing

2. How long it is kept
Retention for inputs, outputs, uploaded files, and logs; how long backups take to clear after deletion
Same item: planned period of processing

3. Where it is stored
Countries or regions where data is processed and stored, and whether you can choose
PDPA Art. 21: international transfers can be restricted in certain cases

4. Which downstream vendors receive it
The subprocessor list, and whether you are notified of changes
Enforcement Rules Art. 8(2)(3): where there is subcontracting, the agreed subcontractors

5. How you are notified
How soon you are told about a breach, what the notice contains, and the remedies
Art. 8(2)(4): matters to be notified and remedies for violations

6. What happens at the end
How data is exported, when it is deleted, and whether you can get proof of deletion
Art. 8(2)(6): return of data media and deletion of stored data when the commission ends

Article 8(3) also requires the commissioning party to regularly confirm how the contractor is performing and to record the results. Article 4 of the Personal Data Protection Act provides that a party commissioned to process personal data is deemed to be the commissioning party within the scope of the Act.

## 2. Four tips for reading the terms

These are practical steps:

- Read the terms for the plan you actually use.  With the same vendor, personal accounts, team plans, enterprise contracts, and the API often have different data conditions. Do not infer your plan's conditions from the brand's general description. Personal accounts employees open themselves are outside the company's control; see [What are the risks when employees paste company data into ChatGPT?](https://thinkbigtw.com/en/qa/employees-chatgpt-company-data/)

- Screenshot and keep the settings.  "Not used for training" is often a switch in the account settings; keep a record of its state at signing.

- Record the terms' version and date.  Terms change; keep the version in force at signing and compare when it is revised.

- Map the data flow.  Note which vendor receives questions, files, indexes, logs, and backups. See [When AI searches company documents, where does the data go?](https://thinkbigtw.com/en/qa/rag-data-flow-cloud-vs-local/)

## 3. What international frameworks say

- NIST AI Risk Management Framework 1.0 : GOVERN 6.1 calls for policies and procedures addressing AI risks from third-party entities; GOVERN 6.2 calls for contingency processes to handle failures or incidents in third-party data or AI systems.

- NIST AI 600-1 (Generative AI Profile) : lists "value chain and component integration" as one of 12 generative AI risks, including non-transparent upstream third-party components and improper supplier vetting across the AI lifecycle.

Brand information | Think BIG

## How Think BIG handles vendor terms during deployment

Think BIG (Think BIG Make it Real CO., LTD.) is an enterprise AI Agent deployment provider headquartered in Taiwan. Starting from protecting company data, we build AI Agents inside the client's own environment (company hardware, or a cloud server under the company's account). There are two deployment options: with the on-premises version, models and documents are processed on company hardware; with the cloud-assisted version, employees' questions and the document passages the system retrieves are sent to the model provider for processing.

- API accounts under the company's name : with the cloud-assisted version, the company applies for the model API under its own account, under the provider's terms, so billing and usage records stay with the company.

- Confirmed before deployment : how a vendor uses input data depends on the product, account, and contract settings adopted, so service processing, retention policy, and training use are each confirmed before deployment.

- Exit procedures agreed upfront : custody of accounts, configuration, data, and logs, and the handover, retention, and deletion procedures at the end of service, are defined in advance.

See [On-premises AI and data sovereignty](https://thinkbigtw.com/guides/local-ai-data/).

## FAQ

Q1: Which data terms should a company check before adopting an AI service? At least six: data use (including model training), retention period, storage region, downstream vendors (subcontracting), breach notification method and timing, and data return and deletion when the contract ends. Q2: What does Taiwan's personal data law require when commissioning an AI vendor to process personal data? Article 8 of the Enforcement Rules of the Personal Data Protection Act requires appropriate oversight of the contractor, covering at least the scope, categories, purpose, and period of processing; the contractor's security measures; subcontracting; notification and remedies for violations; and return and deletion when the commission ends, with regular checks and recorded results. Q3: Is "we don't train on your data" enough? No. You also need to know how long data is kept, where it is stored, which downstream vendors receive it, how breaches are notified, and how data is deleted at the end, and confirm that the statement applies to the plan and account settings you actually use. Q4: What is subcontracting, and why ask about it? Subcontracting is when the vendor passes data to other companies, such as cloud hosts or outsourced support. Article 8 of the Enforcement Rules lists "the agreed subcontractors, where there is subcontracting" as an oversight item, so get the list of downstream vendors and agree to be notified of changes.

- Personal Data Protection Act, Articles 4 and 21, Laws & Regulations Database of Taiwan: [law.moj.gov.tw](https://law.moj.gov.tw/LawClass/LawAll.aspx?pcode=I0050021)

- NIST AI 100-1, Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0) (GOVERN 6.1, 6.2): [nvlpubs.nist.gov](https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/ai/NIST.AI.100-1.pdf)

- NIST AI 600-1, Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative Artificial Intelligence Profile (value chain and component integration): [nvlpubs.nist.gov](https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/ai/NIST.AI.600-1.pdf)

# How to Start Bedtime Reading: 4 Steps to Build a Lasting Bedtime Routine | Think BIG Q&A Library

[← Q&A Library](https://thinkbigtw.com/en/qa/)

Q11

# How to Start Bedtime Reading: 4 Steps to Build a Lasting Bedtime Routine

Think BIG Q&A Library  ·  2026-10-21
      ·  [中文](https://thinkbigtw.com/library/qa/bedtime-reading-routine/)

The short answer

Bedtime reading can start with 4 steps: set a fixed bedtime, arrange a fixed sequence of quiet activities, place the story after going to bed, and end with a fixed phrase before lights out. Taiwan's National Health Administration recommends building a "bedtime ritual" for children, with an example sequence of toilet, bath, pajamas, teeth, water, bed, story, goodnight, lights out; the American Academy of Pediatrics also notes that all children benefit from a regular bedtime routine, such as "brush, book, bed."

## 1. What official sources say

Taiwan's Ministry of Health and Welfare National Health Administration's Maternal and Child Care website writes: establishing a "bedtime ritual" for children helps them fall asleep smoothly—that is, performing a series of quiet preparatory activities in a fixed order before sleep to help children relax, with the example sequence of "toilet → bath → pajamas → teeth → water → bed → story → goodnight → lights out." ([NHA Maternal and Child Care Website](https://mammy.hpa.gov.tw/Home/NewsKBContent?id=3626&type=01))

The American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) HealthyChildren website also notes that all children benefit from a regular bedtime routine; for young children, an early start with "brush, book, bed" in that order is recommended. ([HealthyChildren.org](https://www.healthychildren.org/English/healthy-living/sleep/Pages/Healthy-Sleep-Habits-How-Many-Hours-Does-Your-Child-Need.aspx))

## 2. Four steps

1. Set a fixed bedtime.  The NHA explains that the bedtime is not decided by the child alone, but set by the parent considering the needs of both parent and child, and carried out consistently.

2. Arrange a fixed sequence of quiet activities.  With a fixed sequence, the child knows "what comes next." The NHA example above can be used directly and adjusted to fit your family's habits.

3. Place the story after going to bed, before lights out.  Read slowly and softly. For book selection, the Ministry of Education Bookstart Reading Handbook notes that children aged 2–3 like to look at the same book repeatedly and are suited to picture books with simple plots, repetitive sentence patterns, and content about everyday experiences such as eating, bathing, brushing teeth, and sleeping. ([Bookstart Reading Handbook](https://wwwacc.ntl.edu.tw/public/Attachment/16715141325.pdf)) So reading the same book every night is fine.

4. End with a fixed phrase.  Tell the child in advance that "after this book we say goodnight and turn off the lights," and close the book when it is done. This is a practical recommendation, not from the above sources; the closing phrase is yours to choose—the key is to use the same one every day.

## 3. Common sticking points

The child keeps asking for one more book.  The NHA also mentions that most children like to play and don't want to go to bed, and bedtime struggles are common. Agreeing in advance on "how many books tonight" is easier than refusing in the moment.

Too tired today to read.  The routine can be shortened, but try to keep the order: teeth, bed, a short story, goodnight.

Brand information | Tale With You

Every page is slower and quieter; by the last page, it is just right to fall asleep.

## FAQ

The NHA recommends building a "bedtime ritual," with an example sequence including teeth, bed, story, goodnight, and lights out. Q2: What is a bedtime ritual? # Will Learning Two Languages at Once Make My Child Talk Later? | Q&A Library | Think BIG

[← Q&A Library](https://thinkbigtw.com/en/qa/)

熊好學 · BearSay Mandarin BS05

# Will Learning Two Languages at Once Make My Child Talk Later?

Think BIG Q&A Library　·　November 9, 2026 　·　[中文版](https://thinkbigtw.com/library/qa/bilingual-children-language-delay/)

Short answer

Learning two languages at once can look slower in each single language, but that does not mean overall language development is behind. Hoff and colleagues (2012) compared bilingual and monolingual children aged 22 to 30 months: in a single-language comparison the monolingual children were ahead in vocabulary and grammar, but on total vocabulary across both languages the groups were comparable. Within the bilingual group, performance in each language was related to how much input the child got in that language. If you are still worried about your child's language, a child-development or speech-language professional can assess it, so you do not have to judge on your own.

## 1. What the study did

Hoff, Core, Place, Rumiche, Señor and Parra (2012) compared bilingual and monolingual children from equivalently high-SES families, aged from 1 year 10 months to 2 years 6 months, on vocabulary and grammar. ([Journal of Child Language, 2012](https://doi.org/10.1017/S0305000910000759))

Comparison Result
A single language (for example English only) Monolingual children scored higher in vocabulary and grammar

Total vocabulary across both languages The groups were comparable

Within the bilingual group Vocabulary and grammar in each language were related to the relative amount of input in that language

## 2. How to read it

"Slower" refers to one language alone.  A bilingual child's words are spread over two languages, so each language on its own looks smaller.

Amount of input matters.  Performance in each language is tied to how much of it the child hears, so a child who should progress in Mandarin needs enough steady Mandarin input.

It is one study.  It covers specific ages and family conditions and cannot cover every situation.

Do not delay an assessment.  If a child is clearly behind same-age peers in both languages, see a professional instead of assuming "that's just bilingualism."

## 3. What parents can do

1. Secure Mandarin input.  Fixed people, fixed times or fixed settings give the child steady Mandarin to hear.

2. Use both languages in real conversation.  See [practising speaking at home](https://thinkbigtw.com/en/qa/practice-speaking-at-home/).

3. Avoid single-language comparisons.  Look at both languages together rather than comparing one language with other children.

Brand information | BearSay Mandarin

## BearSay Mandarin and bilingual children

Every day it teaches one Taiwan Mandarin word on Instagram ([@bearsaymandarin](https://www.instagram.com/bearsaymandarin/)), in Traditional characters with zhuyin and pinyin and multilingual subtitles, guided by five characters: BUBU, MIBO, HUBO, GUIBO and LANBO. The app is in development and has not been released. Release information will appear on the [BearSay Mandarin Q&A overview](https://thinkbigtw.com/en/qa/bearsay/).

BearSay Mandarin's daily word comes with multilingual subtitles, which can be one way for bilingual or multilingual families to meet Taiwan Mandarin. If you are concerned about a child's language development, consult a professional. BearSay Mandarin does not diagnose and does not guarantee any learning result.

Source: the public Instagram account and this site's brand overview, updated 2026-11-09. Demo audio is AI-synthesized speech; BearSay Mandarin characters are AI-generated.

## Frequently asked questions

Q1: Will learning two languages make my child talk later? Hoff et al. (2012) compared children aged 22 to 30 months: in a single language, monolingual children were ahead in vocabulary and grammar, but total vocabulary across both languages was comparable. So bilingualism cannot simply be said to cause overall delay. Q2: Why does my bilingual child seem to know fewer Mandarin words? Words are spread over two languages. The study also found performance in each language was related to how much input the child got in it. Q3: How can I help a bilingual child's Mandarin? Give steady Mandarin to hear and use, such as fixed people, times or settings, with real conversation. This advice follows the study's findings and is not a guarantee. Q4: When should I ask a professional? If a child is clearly behind same-age peers in both languages, or you stay concerned, ask a child-development or speech-language professional for an assessment.

# Do Bilingual Picture Books Help Children? How to Read Them Together at Home | Think BIG Q&A Library

[← Q&A Library](https://thinkbigtw.com/en/qa/)

Shared Reading & Custom Picture Books
Q15

# Do Bilingual Picture Books Help Children? How to Read Them Together at Home

Think BIG Q&A Library  ·  2026-10-25
      ·  [中文](https://thinkbigtw.com/library/qa/bilingual-picture-books/)

The short answer

Bilingual picture books may be helpful, but the existing evidence is limited. A randomized study had 22 Spanish-speaking children aged 4–6 who were learning English receive two types of word explanations during book reading, 2 weeks each; in the weeks with home-language (Spanish) explanations, children learned more vocabulary than in the weeks with English-only explanations. However, the study was small, the language combination was not Chinese-English, and it cannot be directly used as evidence that Chinese-English bilingual picture books are definitely effective. At home, start with the language the child is familiar with; add English sentences as supplementary.

## 1. What one study found

Lugo-Neris, Jackson, and Goldstein (2010) studied 22 Spanish-speaking children aged 4–6 who were learning English. During weeks when explanations were given in Spanish (their home language), children acquired more English vocabulary than during weeks when explanations were given in English. The researchers concluded that using the home language to explain book content can support second-language vocabulary learning. ([Language, Speech, and Hearing Services in Schools, 2010](https://doi.org/10.1044/1058-0360(2010/08-0019)))

## 2. What this study did not say

The sample was small.  The study had 22 children, all Spanish-speaking preschoolers learning English in the United States. The findings should not be directly applied to all language combinations or family environments.

The language environment is different.  Taiwan's situation—Mandarin as the home language, English as a foreign language—is different from the study's context. Whether the same findings apply needs further examination.

## 3. What Taiwan's 2030 Bilingual Policy says

The Executive Yuan's 2030 Bilingual Policy aims for citizens to be able to use both Mandarin and English in their daily lives and work; it does not mandate at what age children must start or which method parents should use. ([Executive Yuan 2030 Bilingual Policy](https://www.ey.gov.tw/Page/5A8A0CB5B41DA11E))

The AAP's 2024 policy statement in Pediatrics encourages parents to read and converse with children from infancy in the language they are most comfortable with; it also affirms that growing up bilingual does not cause language delays. ([Pediatrics 2024](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39342414/))

## 4. 4 practical steps

1. Use the language you are more comfortable with.  The AAP's recommendation is to read in the language you are most comfortable with; a smooth and natural read makes for better shared reading.

2. Try the home-language explanation method.  Point to the picture, name the item in English, then say it once more in Mandarin. This follows the direction of the study: explaining in the home language may help the child understand the new language word.

3. Don't require the child to respond in a specific language.  Let the child respond in whichever language they like; don't interrupt the story to correct their language.

4. Repeat frequently.  Repetition is the key to vocabulary acquisition; reading the same bilingual book several times is more effective than briefly reading many books.

## 5. Limitations to keep in mind

This article is based primarily on one study; the findings are preliminary and should not be treated as a definitive conclusion. Family language environment, the child's age, and exposure time all affect results. If you have specific concerns about bilingual development, it is recommended to consult a speech-language pathologist or related specialist.

Brand information | Tale With You

A randomized study showed that when home-language (Spanish) word explanations were used during English book reading, children learned more vocabulary than English-only; but the study only had 22 children, and the language combination was Spanish-English, so it cannot be directly applied to Chinese-English. Q2: How should I read Chinese-English bilingual books at home? # How to Pick a Birthday Gift Book a Child Will Read Again and Again | Think BIG Q&A Library

[← Q&A Library](https://thinkbigtw.com/en/qa/)

Shared Reading & Custom Picture Books
Q10

# How to Pick a Birthday Gift Book a Child Will Read Again and Again

Think BIG Q&A Library  ·  2026-10-20
      ·  [中文](https://thinkbigtw.com/library/qa/birthday-gift-picture-book/)

The short answer

When choosing a birthday gift for a child, first look at three things: what the child is currently interested in, whether the gift can be enjoyed together—played with or read—and whether safety has been covered. If choosing a toy, the Bureau of Standards, Metrology and Inspection (BSMI) recommends looking for the "Product Inspection Mark" and checking the Chinese-language label and recommended age; if choosing a book, choose content based on the child's familiar everyday situations, and also something the adult can read through, because children will keep pulling it out to ask for another read.

## 1. Three questions to ask first

1. What is the child into right now?  A gift that matches what the child is currently interested in is more likely to become something they reach for every day.

2. Can two people enjoy it together?  The American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) 2024 policy statement states that reading regularly with infants and young children strengthens the parent–child relationship and is a foundation for social-emotional, cognitive, language, and literacy development; it recommends starting from birth and continuing at least through kindergarten. ([Pediatrics 2024](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39342414/))

3. Is it safe?  Young children put things in their mouths and pull, tug, and drop them; check for safety before buying.

## 2. If choosing a toy: 7 reminders from BSMI

In a September 2023 announcement (originally covering products such as children's soft building blocks), the Bureau of Standards, Metrology and Inspection (BSMI) reminded parents to note the following when buying and using toys. ([BSMI press materials](https://safety.bsmi.gov.tw/wSite/public/Attachment/f1695861288403.pdf))

- Only buy toys bearing the Product Inspection Mark.

- Check for a detailed Chinese-language label; read the recommended age, precautions, warnings, and usage instructions carefully.

- Choose toys suitable for the child's age.

- Do not let infants and young children put toys in their mouths or chew on them; wash hands after playing.

- Check that the toy structure is complete, the surface is smooth, and all parts are secure; if there are small parts, sharp edges, rough edges, or accessible pointed tips, do not give the toy to a child.

- Toys containing magnetic accessories (such as magnets or magnetic beads) should not be given to infants and young children, to prevent accidental swallowing.

- Soft plastic bags or films used as packaging should be discarded or stored out of the child's reach immediately after unpacking.

## 3. If choosing a book: 3 things to consider

1. Choose content based on familiar everyday situations.  The Ministry of Education Bookstart Reading Handbook describes children aged 2–3 as having "basic cause-and-effect understanding" and "looking at the same book repeatedly"; books suited to them have simple plots, repetitive sentence patterns, and content about everyday experiences such as eating, bathing, brushing teeth, sleeping, and visiting the doctor. ([Bookstart Reading Handbook](https://wwwacc.ntl.edu.tw/public/Attachment/16715141325.pdf))

2. Expect the child to ask "read it again."  The same book will be read over and over; the book needs to hold up to repetition and have enough in it to keep the adult willing to repeat it too. The same handbook recommends choosing a book "that the grown-up also finds interesting," because a book even the adult finds boring makes it hard to feel motivated to read aloud.

3. Let the child find themselves in the book.  For research on personalized books and their limitations, see [Do books where children are the main character really help with reading?](https://thinkbigtw.com/en/qa/personalized-book-research/)

## 4. Allow time

Birthday gifts come with a date. For gifts that need to be made (such as custom products), factor in both production and shipping time, plus a small buffer for preview confirmation. See [how long custom picture books take](https://thinkbigtw.com/en/qa/custom-book-lead-time/); the specific schedule varies by provider.

# My Child Says They Want to Be Something When They Grow Up: How to Nurture Career Curiosity | Think BIG Q&A Library

[← Q&A Library](https://thinkbigtw.com/en/qa/)

Shared Reading & Custom Picture Books
Q22

# My Child Says They Want to Be Something When They Grow Up: How to Nurture Career Curiosity

Think BIG Q&A Library  ·  2026-11-01
      ·  [中文](https://thinkbigtw.com/library/qa/career-awareness-kids/)

The short answer

Starting career awareness for preschoolers can begin with two steps: "picture books first, then try it out." Read picture books about occupations first to let the child come into contact with more types of jobs; then find one job in their daily environment to observe or experience. The National Academy for Educational Research's 2020 Career Education Handbook states that career awareness at the preschool stage is about exposure and experience, not training for a future job.

## 1. What the curriculum framework says

The Ministry of Education's Preschool Curriculum Framework (social domain) lists "understanding people and environments" as a learning dimension, including understanding people's roles and activities, cultural customs and festivals, and diverse ways of living in the community. Occupations are one type of people's role. The curriculum objective is to "recognize the diverse phenomena of culture in the living environment"—not to prepare for a particular career. ([Ministry of Education Legal Information](https://edu.law.moe.gov.tw/LawContent.aspx?id=GL001586))

The National Academy for Educational Research's Career Education Implementation Handbook (2020) states that career awareness at the preschool stage focuses on exposure and experience, allowing children to understand what occupations exist through daily life, play, and stories, rather than developing specific skills. ([NAER Handbook](https://cirn.moe.edu.tw/Upload/file/27366/90736.pdf))

## 2. Picture books first, then try it out

Step 1: Choose picture books about daily occupations.  Doctors, bakers, train drivers, farmers—any occupation the child encounters in daily life is worth reading about. After reading, ask "what did this person do today?" to help the child organize what they learned.

Step 2: Find one job in the living environment to observe.  The delivery person who comes to the house, the person at the community convenience store, the cleaner at the park—these are people with jobs that the child can actually observe. After observing, connect it back to the picture book: "This is similar to the baker in the book, right?"

Step 3: Let the child try it out in play.  NAER's handbook points to play as one of the main ways preschoolers experience occupations. Set up a "store" at home, let the child be the cook, let toys be customers. Trying it out is more effective for understanding than explaining.

## 3. What not to rush

Career awareness at the preschool stage is "this occupation exists, this person does this kind of work." Asking "what do you want to be when you grow up?" is a question to leave for later; answering it too early may cause children to narrow their range of exploration. The NAER handbook also emphasizes letting children freely explore different types of work rather than guiding them toward a specific answer.

# Giving a Custom Book to a Friend's Child: How Do You Get the Photos, and Who Do You Ask First? | Think BIG Q&A Library

[← Q&A Library](https://thinkbigtw.com/en/qa/)

Shared Reading & Custom Picture Books
Q29

# Giving a Custom Book to a Friend's Child: How Do You Get the Photos, and Who Do You Ask First?

Think BIG Q&A Library  ·  2026-11-08
      ·  [中文](https://thinkbigtw.com/library/qa/custom-book-gift-for-friends-kid/)

The short answer

Ordering a custom picture book as a gift for a friend's child requires the consent and participation of the child's parents or guardians. The photo used in the book is personal data; under Taiwan's Personal Data Protection Act, the person providing personal data must consent, and for a minor, consent must be given by a parent or legal guardian. When a third party orders, the person placing the order is not the data subject's guardian, so the child's parent must be involved in uploading the photo and confirming the preview.

## 1. Why the child's parents must be involved

Under Civil Code Article 1086, parents are the legal representatives of a minor child. For a child's photo—which is personal data under the Personal Data Protection Act (PDPA) Article 2—the person who can decide how to use it is the child's parent or guardian, not a third party.

PDPA Article 7 requires that the collection of personal data be with the data subject's consent; Article 8 requires that the collecting party notify the data subject of the purpose, categories, period, territory, recipients, and methods of use, as well as the data subject's rights. For a minor, the parent or guardian gives this consent. So even if you want to give a gift, you cannot simply take the child's photo and place an order without the parents knowing. ([Personal Data Protection Act](https://law.moj.gov.tw/LawClass/LawAll.aspx?pcode=I0050021), [Civil Code](https://law.moj.gov.tw/LawClass/LawAll.aspx?pcode=B0000001))

## 2. How to handle it in practice

Step 1: Notify the child's parents first.  Tell them you want to give this gift and ask if they are willing to cooperate. Don't collect photos before asking.

Step 2: Let the parents provide the photo.  Photos should come from the child's parent directly, not from group photos or social media. The parents should read the provider's privacy policy and photo usage instructions.

Step 3: Let the parents confirm the preview.  The preview is a low-resolution watermarked image of the cover and some interior pages. The parents should confirm the character's appearance, the child's name and nickname, and the dedication text. Any adjustments should be communicated through the parents.

Step 4: Coordinate the delivery address.  You can pay, but the delivery address can be to the recipient's family or to your own address for forwarding; decide in advance and inform the parents.

## 3. What about providers' own rules

Some providers specify that only the child's parents or guardians may place orders and upload photos. Check the provider's terms of service before ordering to confirm whether third-party ordering is accepted and what the specific process is.

Brand information | Tale With You

Article 19 specifies that photos are submitted through Shopee chat after the order is placed.

If you would like to order as a gift for a friend's child, you need to have the child's parent or guardian place the order (or authorize you clearly), upload the photo, and confirm the preview. It is recommended to coordinate with the parents first before placing the order.

Q1: Can I order a custom picture book as a gift for a friend's child? You can pay, but the child's parent or guardian must be involved in uploading the photo and confirming the preview. Under the Personal Data Protection Act, the person who can consent to the use of a child's photo is the parent or guardian. Q2: Can I use a photo from a group photo or social media? It is not recommended. Photos should come directly from the child's parent; it is best to let the parent select the photo and read the provider's privacy policy before providing it. Q3: Why can't a third party place the order on behalf of the child? # How Long Does a Custom Picture Book Take? How to Plan the Order Before a Holiday | Think BIG Q&A Library
