# What Are the Security Risks of Generative AI? The OWASP LLM Top 10 (2025) at a Glance | Q&A Library | Think BIG

[← Q&A Library](https://thinkbigtw.com/en/qa/)

Enterprise AI Security
TB19

# What Are the Security Risks of Generative AI? The OWASP LLM Top 10 (2025) at a Glance

Think BIG Q&A Library  ·  2026-11-01
      ·  [中文](https://thinkbigtw.com/library/qa/owasp-llm-top10-overview/)

The short answer

The 2025 OWASP Top 10 for LLM applications is: LLM01 Prompt Injection, LLM02 Sensitive Information Disclosure, LLM03 Supply Chain, LLM04 Data and Model Poisoning, LLM05 Improper Output Handling, LLM06 Excessive Agency, LLM07 System Prompt Leakage, LLM08 Vector and Embedding Weaknesses, LLM09 Misinformation, and LLM10 Unbounded Consumption. When a company deploys AI Agents and document Q&A, it can start with LLM01, LLM02, LLM06, and LLM08, because they bear directly on whether data leaks and whether the AI takes actions it should not.

## 1. All ten at a glance

ID
Risk
In one line
What to do
LLM01
Prompt Injection
Input alters the model's behavior or output; instructions can hide in documents or web pages the AI reads and need not be visible to people.
[What is prompt injection?](https://thinkbigtw.com/en/qa/prompt-injection-ai-agent/)

LLM02
Sensitive Information Disclosure
Personal, financial, health, confidential business data, or credentials leak through the model's output.
[De-identifying data before AI](https://thinkbigtw.com/en/qa/deidentify-before-ai/), [Risks of employees pasting company data into ChatGPT](https://thinkbigtw.com/en/qa/employees-chatgpt-company-data/)

LLM03
Supply Chain
Weaknesses in training data, models, and deployment platforms, including third-party pre-trained models and data, not just code packages.
[What a pre-delivery security review checks](https://thinkbigtw.com/en/qa/ai-agent-pre-delivery-security-review/), [License checks for open models](https://thinkbigtw.com/en/qa/open-model-license-checklist/)

LLM04
Data and Model Poisoning
Pre-training, fine-tuning, or embedding data is tampered with to plant weaknesses, backdoors, or bias; model files from shared repositories can also carry malicious code.
[Updating models in an offline environment](https://thinkbigtw.com/en/qa/offline-local-llm-updates/)

LLM05
Improper Output Handling
Model output is passed to downstream systems without validation or sanitization.
Treat AI output as untrusted input and validate it before downstream use ([OWASP LLM05](https://genai.owasp.org/llmrisk/llm052025-improper-output-handling/))

LLM06
Excessive Agency
An AI Agent has too many tools, permissions, or autonomy, so a model error causes damage.
[How should AI Agent permissions be set?](https://thinkbigtw.com/en/qa/ai-agent-permissions/)

LLM07
System Prompt Leakage
The system prompt contains things it should not; OWASP stresses that system prompts should not be treated as secrets or security controls, and credentials or connection strings must not be in them.
[What happens if an AI API key leaks?](https://thinkbigtw.com/en/qa/ai-api-key-leak/)

LLM08
Vector and Embedding Weaknesses
In RAG (retrieval-augmented generation), weaknesses in how vectors and embeddings are generated, stored, or retrieved can expose data people should not see.
[Making sure each department sees only its own data](https://thinkbigtw.com/en/qa/rag-access-control-by-department/)

LLM09
Misinformation
The model produces content that looks credible but is wrong; overreliance without verification makes the harm worse.
[When AI is wrong but sounds confident](https://thinkbigtw.com/en/news/ai-hallucination-20261012/)

LLM10
Unbounded Consumption
Users can call the model excessively and without control, causing outages, runaway costs, or even model cloning.
[What happens if an AI API key leaks?](https://thinkbigtw.com/en/qa/ai-api-key-leak/) (spend limits)

The "In one line" column is a plain summary of each OWASP description; the "What to do" column links to in-depth answers in the Q&A Library.

## 2. Why start with LLM01, 02, 06, and 08

These are practical reasons for the order:

- LLM01 and LLM06 go together.  Prompt injection makes the AI do something it should not; the more permission an AI Agent has, the worse the result. Narrowing permissions and requiring human approval for important actions lowers both risks.

- LLM02 and LLM08 go together.  Once company documents are searchable by AI, who can see what must be controlled at retrieval, not only through prompts.

- All four can happen whether the model runs on-premises or in the cloud. See [What are the drawbacks of a local LLM?](https://thinkbigtw.com/en/qa/local-llm-limitations/)

## 3. How it differs from NIST's generative AI risk list

OWASP's list names weaknesses and countermeasures from the angle of building and deploying LLM applications. NIST AI 600-1 (Generative AI Profile) lists 12 generative AI risks from the angle of organizational risk management, such as confabulation, data privacy, information security, and value chain and component integration. The two work together: OWASP for checking systems, NIST for building management practices. For managing third-party vendors, see [Which points in an AI vendor's data terms should you check?](https://thinkbigtw.com/en/qa/ai-vendor-data-terms/); for handling incidents, see [What should a company do when an AI system has a security incident?](https://thinkbigtw.com/en/qa/ai-incident-response/)

Brand information | Think BIG

## Think BIG's pre-delivery security review

Think BIG (Think BIG Make it Real CO., LTD.) is an enterprise AI Agent deployment provider headquartered in Taiwan. Starting from protecting company data, we build AI Agents inside the client's own environment (company hardware, or a cloud server under the company's account). There are two deployment options: with the on-premises version, models and documents are processed on company hardware; with the cloud-assisted version, employees' questions and the document passages the system retrieves are sent to the model provider for processing.

- Pre-delivery security review : before each system is delivered, its code and configuration go through a security review: comparing the exact version to be delivered, checking outbound connections and permissions, and confirming keys are not exposed. If it does not pass, it is not delivered.

- Third-party components and keys : third-party packages are reviewed for source and license, pinned, and not auto-updated. Keys stay in permission-protected configuration files, never in the repository or in chat.

- Permissions enforced at retrieval : permissions must be enforced when content is retrieved, not only by writing "do not disclose" in a prompt.

No one can promise perfect security; what we do is review, one gate at a time. See [Trust](https://thinkbigtw.com/trust/).

The actual scope of Think BIG's services follows what both parties confirm.

## FAQ

Q1: What is the OWASP LLM Top 10? The OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications is a list from OWASP, an open international application security community, of the ten most important security risks and countermeasures in building and deploying large language model applications; the 2025 edition is the current one. In December 2025 OWASP also published the Top 10 for Agentic Applications 2026, which focuses on autonomous AI Agents. Q2: What are the ten items in the 2025 edition? LLM01 Prompt Injection, LLM02 Sensitive Information Disclosure, LLM03 Supply Chain, LLM04 Data and Model Poisoning, LLM05 Improper Output Handling, LLM06 Excessive Agency, LLM07 System Prompt Leakage, LLM08 Vector and Embedding Weaknesses, LLM09 Misinformation, and LLM10 Unbounded Consumption. Q3: Does a local LLM remove these risks? No. On-premises deployment decides whether data leaves the company; prompt injection, excessive agency, vector and embedding weaknesses, and misinformation can happen wherever the model runs, and are handled with permission design, human approval, and testing. Q4: How do the OWASP and NIST lists differ? The OWASP LLM Top 10 lists weaknesses and countermeasures from the angle of building and deploying applications; NIST AI 600-1 lists 12 generative AI risks from the angle of organizational risk management. The first suits checking systems; the second suits building management practices.

- OWASP LLM06:2025 Excessive Agency: [genai.owasp.org](https://genai.owasp.org/llmrisk/llm062025-excessive-agency/)

- OWASP LLM07:2025 System Prompt Leakage: [genai.owasp.org](https://genai.owasp.org/llmrisk/llm072025-system-prompt-leakage/)

# Can Parents Be Drawn Into a Custom Picture Book Too? What to Know When Adults Are in the Photo | Think BIG Q&A Library

[← Q&A Library](https://thinkbigtw.com/en/qa/)

Shared Reading & Custom Picture Books
Q17

# Can Parents Be Drawn Into a Custom Picture Book Too? What to Know When Adults Are in the Photo

Think BIG Q&A Library  ·  2026-10-27
      ·  [中文](https://thinkbigtw.com/library/qa/parents-in-custom-book/)

The short answer

Yes, but an adult's photo is also personal data, so the person in the photo must give their own consent first. Using Tale With You as an example, you can optionally submit photos of 1–2 adults, 1–2 solo photos per adult, at no extra charge; the main character is still the child. Any adult appearing in photos must be an adult who gives their own consent. If the second adult (such as the other parent or a grandparent) is someone other than the person placing the order, their consent must be obtained first. Before ordering you can also ask the provider how they obtain consent from other adults in the photos — for example, whether consent must be given directly by that person.

## 1. Why an adult's photo also requires that person's consent

The Personal Data Protection Act Article 2 lists "characteristics" and "other data that can directly or indirectly identify an individual" as personal data ([Laws and Regulations Database](https://law.moj.gov.tw/LawClass/LawAll.aspx?pcode=I0050021)). A front-facing photo of a father or mother, just like a child's photo, can directly identify who that person is.

For a provider (a "non-public entity" in legal terms) to collect personal data, Article 19 requires a specific purpose and compliance with one of the statutory conditions, such as having a contractual relationship with the data subject or obtaining the data subject's consent. The adult in the photo is not necessarily the person placing the order and may not have a contract with the provider, so the question is whether that adult has given their own consent.

Therefore, before placing an order, confirm how the provider obtains consent from other adults in the photos — for example, whether that adult must express consent directly. Additionally, Article 8 lists what a provider must notify when collecting personal data: the name of the collecting entity, the purpose of collection, the category of data, the period, territory, recipients, and methods of use, and the rights the data subject may exercise; this can be checked against the provider's privacy policy.

Adults themselves also have rights under Article 3: to inquire, view, request deletion, request cessation of collection, processing, or use, and so on; these rights cannot be waived in advance by contract.

## 2. 5 things to confirm before ordering

- Who will appear?  First count clearly which adults will appear, then check how many the provider can illustrate at one time.

- Has every person consented? How does the provider confirm?  It is simplest when only the person placing the order appears; for another parent or elder to appear, first explain the photo's purpose and the deletion process to them and get their agreement before submitting. Also ask the provider how they obtain consent from other adults in the photos — for example, whether consent must be given directly by that person.

- Does each photo show only that adult?  Do not use a group photo, to avoid submitting someone who hasn't consented.

- Which pages will the adult appear on?  In a custom picture book the main character is usually the child; ask in advance which pages the adult will appear on based on the story, to avoid unmet expectations.

- What if the adult changes their mind?  Ask the provider whether the adult in the photo can apply to have their data deleted themselves, and how that is handled before and after printing.

For questions about a child's photos, see [How is privacy protected when using a child's photo for a custom picture book?](https://thinkbigtw.com/en/qa/photo-privacy-custom-book/) This page covers only adults' photos.

Brand information | Tale With You

## How Tale With You handles adults appearing in the book

Tale With You's [Privacy Policy](https://talewithyoutw.com/privacy.html) and [Terms of Service](https://talewithyoutw.com/terms.html) (v1.3, updated 10 October 2026) state the following about adults appearing in the book:

- May appear, same price:  Optional. 1–2 adults, 1–2 solo front-facing photos per adult, with only that adult in the photo. The adult will appear as an AI illustration in the book; which pages they appear on depends on the story; the main character is still the child.

- Personal consent required:  Any adult appearing in photos must be an adult who gives their own consent. When a second adult (such as the other parent or a grandparent) is involved, the person placing the order must first obtain that adult's consent and show them the explanation in the "children's photo consent form." The person placing the order can also ask the provider how they obtain consent from other adults in the photos — for example, whether consent must be given directly by that person.

- Only illustrates faces of adults who have submitted photos:  In scenes that require an adult's presence (or when no adult photo has been submitted), the adult is drawn from behind, in profile, or from the shoulders down — no unfamiliar adult's face will be drawn.

- Same handling as the child's photos:  Used only for this one book, not for advertisements. The OpenAI account used for production has had "improve the model with data" disabled; according to OpenAI's documentation, after disabling this setting, new conversations will not be used to train their model. All files for this order are deleted within 3 days of the book's delivery. Data OpenAI retains under its own policy, as well as messages on the Shopee or LINE platforms, are outside the deletion scope; see the [Privacy Policy](https://talewithyoutw.com/privacy.html) for details.

- The adult can apply for deletion directly:  The adult in the photo can contact the provider directly via the official LINE or Email to request deletion or withdrawal of consent. If the request is made before printing, their photo will be deleted and their face will no longer be illustrated; the person who placed the order may also choose to cancel the order for a full refund. If the book has already been sent for printing or shipped, the physical book cannot be recalled.

The illustration is drawn by AI based on the photo and may not exactly match the person's appearance; a preview will be sent for confirmation before printing. If the adult's illustration is not a close likeness, the free regeneration included with each order can be used, or the option to not illustrate the adult's face can be chosen.

Content in this section is taken from the Tale With You website's Privacy Policy, Terms of Service, and FAQ, verified on 2026-10-24. All characters in books and videos are AI-generated.

## FAQ

Q1: Can parents both appear together in a custom picture book? Yes, but it depends on the provider's rules. Using Tale With You as an example, you can optionally submit 1–2 adults with 1–2 solo photos per adult at no extra charge; the main character is still the child; any adult in the photos must be an adult who gives their own consent. Q2: If you upload a photo of your partner or an elder, is their consent needed? Yes. A front-facing adult photo is also personal data. Using Tale With You as an example, when a second adult is involved, the person placing the order must first obtain that adult's consent; you can also ask the provider how consent from other adults in the photos is obtained — for example, whether it must be given directly by that person. Q3: Can the adult in the photo later request deletion? Yes. Personal Data Protection Act Article 3 guarantees the data subject's right to request deletion and cessation of collection, processing, or use. Using Tale With You as an example, the adult in the photo can apply directly; before printing, their photo will be deleted and their face will no longer be illustrated; once the book has been sent for printing or shipped, the physical book cannot be recalled. Q4: If no adult photo is submitted, will an adult appear in the book? Using Tale With You as an example, in scenes requiring an adult's presence, the adult is drawn from behind, in profile, or from the shoulders down — no unfamiliar adult's face will be drawn; an adult's face in the book is illustrated only from the submitted photo.

# Do Books Starring Your Child Really Help With Reading? What the Research Says | Think BIG Q&A Library

[← Q&A Library](https://thinkbigtw.com/en/qa/)

Shared Reading & Custom Picture Books
Q03

# Do Books Starring Your Child Really Help With Reading? What the Research Says

Think BIG Q&A Library  ·  2026-10-13
      ·  [中文](https://thinkbigtw.com/library/qa/personalized-book-research/)

The short answer

There is preliminary research support. Studies by Kucirkova and colleagues at the Open University in the UK found that 3-year-old children learned new words faster in passages where they themselves were the main character; and when reading a book featuring the child as the main character, smiling, laughter, and talking between parent and child were also noticeably more frequent. However, these studies were very small in scale; they can better be said to show "greater engagement" rather than proving that long-term reading ability will necessarily improve as a result.

## 1. How the research was conducted

A "personalized picture book" refers to a book made specifically for one child — this may involve putting the child's name, photo, or personal details into the story. The researcher who has studied this topic most extensively is Natalia Kucirkova and colleagues at The Open University in the UK. Two commonly cited studies are as follows:

Study Subjects and methods Findings
Kucirkova, Messer & Sheehy (2014)
First Language , vol. 34 18 children aged 3. The same book contained both "personalized" and "non-personalized" passages, each containing several new words the children didn't know; the book was read together twice over a week, then the children were tested on whether they understood these words. Children learned new words in the personalized passages faster ; repeated shared reading made this effect more pronounced.

Kucirkova, Messer & Whitelock (2013)
Journal of Early Childhood Literacy , vol. 13 no. 4 7 families in the UK, with children aged 12 to 33 months. At home, each of three book types was read in turn: a personalized book made for the child, a similarly themed general book, and the child's favorite book; all sessions were video-recorded and analyzed. When reading the personalized book, children's and parents' smiling and laughter were noticeably more frequent ; children also vocalized more than with the other two types of books. Parents' laughter was mostly in response to their child's.

## 2. How to interpret these results

Sample sizes are very small.  One study had 18 children and one had 7 families, and both were conducted in the UK in English. The results are worth noting but cannot be directly generalized to all children.

The effect is "engagement," not a guaranteed ability outcome.  What the studies measured was short-term speed of learning new words, and the frequency of smiling and talking. There is currently no research proving that "reading personalized picture books" leads to better long-term reading outcomes.

What truly matters is having someone to read with.  The American Academy of Pediatrics' 2014 policy statement notes that regularly reading together with young children strengthens the parent-child relationship and builds language, literacy, and social-emotional skills; it recommends starting from infancy and continuing at least until the child enters kindergarten. ([AAP, Pediatrics 2014](https://doi.org/10.1542/peds.2014-1384)) A book where the child is the main character can serve as a "starting point" to get the child willing to sit down and read together, rather than a replacement for general picture books.

## 3. 4 ways to make a book where the child is the main character work

1. Let the child find "where am I."  Find themselves first, then ask: "What are you doing now?" The child will start telling the story in their own words.

2. Ask often: "If it were you, what would you do?"  The main character is them, so it is easier for them to voice their own thoughts — this is exactly the context in which children talked more in the research.

3. Read the same book more than once.  The children in the First Language study read it twice, and repeated shared reading improved new-word learning. When a child asks for "one more time," that's the opportunity.

4. Bring new words from the book into daily life.  When a cable car or ferry appears in the book, point it out the next time you're out; that's how the word truly becomes theirs.

These studies were small in scale; they better show that children are more engaged rather than proving long-term reading ability will improve. Q2: What are the limitations of personalized picture book research? There is currently no research proving it leads to better long-term reading outcomes. Q3: At what age is it better to start reading with children? # Sharing Your Child's Photo for a Custom Picture Book: 6 Privacy Questions to Ask First | Think BIG Q&A Library

Q02

# Sharing Your Child's Photo for a Custom Picture Book: 6 Privacy Questions to Ask First

Think BIG Q&A Library  ·  2026-10-12
      ·  [中文](https://thinkbigtw.com/library/qa/photo-privacy-custom-book/)

The short answer

Before submitting a child's photo to a custom picture book service, clarify 6 things: what the photos will be used for, whether they will be used to train AI, which companies will process them (and whether they will be sent abroad), how they will be stored, when they will be deleted (and what parts cannot be deleted), and how you can request to view or delete them. Taiwan's Personal Data Protection Act Article 8 requires providers to proactively notify you of these matters when collecting personal data; Article 3 guarantees your rights to inquire, stop use, and request deletion, and these rights cannot be waived in advance by contract.

## 1. Why a child's photo needs special care

A front-facing photo of a child can directly identify who that person is. The Personal Data Protection Act Article 2 lists "characteristics" and "other data that can directly or indirectly identify an individual" as personal data ([Laws and Regulations Database](https://law.moj.gov.tw/LawClass/LawAll.aspx?pcode=I0050021)), so photos used in a custom picture book are regulated by the PDPA from the moment they are uploaded.

Another reason is that the child cannot decide for themselves yet. The parents are making this book, but the person in the photo is the child; when choosing a service, thinking "if this photo were to be leaked, would my child mind when they grow up?" helps avoid overlooking important questions.

The Basic AI Act, promulgated and implemented on 14 January 2026, Article 4 also lists "privacy protection and data governance" as one of the principles of AI development, requiring that personal data be properly protected and that data minimization  (collecting and using only necessary data) be applied ([Laws and Regulations Database](https://law.moj.gov.tw/LawClass/LawAll.aspx?pcode=H0160093)). This can serve as a reference standard for choosing an AI custom service.

## 2. 6 things to clarify before ordering

What to ask Why to ask Legal basis
1. What will the photos be used for?
Only for making this one book, or also for advertisements, portfolios, and website samples? The narrower the stated use, the better. Broad language like "may be used for marketing" means the child's face could appear somewhere you hadn't anticipated. PDPA Article 5: use may not exceed what is necessary for the specific purpose

2. Will they be used to train AI? AI picture books require submitting photos to an AI service. Ask at two levels: whether the provider itself will use them for training, and whether the AI service the provider uses has training disabled. PDPA Article 5 (use beyond the stated purpose)

3. Which companies will receive them? Will they be sent abroad? AI services, cloud hosting, printers, and logistics may all handle the data. Many AI services are based overseas, meaning the data will be processed outside Taiwan. PDPA Article 8: must notify of the period, territory, recipients, and methods of use; Article 4: a party entrusted with processing is treated the same as the entrusting party

4. How will they be stored? Who can access them? Whether they are encrypted, where they are stored, and who can open them. Whether preview images are low-resolution and watermarked. PDPA Article 20-1: providers holding personal data must implement security maintenance measures (added November 2025, implementation date to be set by the Executive Yuan)

5. When will they be deleted? What cannot be deleted? There should be a specific time (such as "within X days of delivery"), and it should be clear what is exempt: chat records on messaging apps, data the AI service provider retains under its own policy, and invoice records required by law. PDPA Article 11: when the specific purpose disappears or the period expires, data must be proactively deleted

6. How can I request to view or delete the data? Who to contact, through what channel, and within what timeframe. If another adult also appears in the photos, that adult should also be able to apply. PDPA Article 3: rights to inquire, view, copy, correct, stop use, and delete — these cannot be waived in advance or limited by contract

A reputable provider should have answers to all 6 questions in their privacy policy. If answers are missing or vaguely written, ask for clarification before ordering.

## 3. 3 things parents can do themselves

1. Only submit the necessary photos.  Include only your own child in the photos, not other children; submit only as many photos as the provider requests.

2. Send photos through the provider's designated official channel.  Do not post the child's photos in public comments or on social media posts.

3. After receiving the book, remember the deletion.  Check it against the deletion timeline the provider stated; to request early deletion, you can submit a request directly under PDPA Article 3.

## FAQ

Q1: Is it safe to use a child's photo for a custom picture book? Whether it is safe depends on how the provider handles the photos. Before ordering, confirm 6 things: the purpose of the photos, whether they will be used to train AI, which companies will process them, how they will be stored, when they will be deleted, and how to request viewing or deletion. These are all matters that PDPA Article 8 requires providers to notify. Q2: If the provider says photos will be deleted, does that mean everything is deleted? Not necessarily. # What Kind of Picture Books Suit Each Stage from 0 to 5 Years Old? | Think BIG Q&A Library

Q14

# What Kind of Picture Books Suit Each Stage from 0 to 5 Years Old?

Think BIG Q&A Library  ·  2026-10-24
      ·  [中文](https://thinkbigtw.com/library/qa/picture-books-by-age/)

The short answer

Picture books can be chosen according to a child's developmental stage: ages 0–6 months suit toy books and cloth books with vivid colors and large patterns; ages 6–12 months suit thick board books that are easy to hold and turn; ages 1–2 suit books with large illustrations and few words that relate to everyday life; ages 2–3 suit stories with simple plots and repetitive sentences; ages 3–5 add humorous, emotional, and informational books. This is a summary from the Ministry of Education's Bookstart handbook; age is only a reference — the child's interest and their mood that day matter more.

## 1. How to choose for each stage

Since 2009 (Year 98 of the Republic of China), the Ministry of Education has promoted Bookstart (閱讀起步走), encouraging parent-child shared reading for children ages 0–5, and commissioned the National Taiwan Library to select outstanding books each year and compile reading handbooks; recommended booklists and handbooks from each year can be found on the [National Taiwan Library's Bookstart page](https://wwwacc.ntl.edu.tw/np.asp?ctNode=1399&mp=14). The table below is adapted from the "Infant and Toddler Development Characteristics and Shared Reading Strategy Reference Table" in the appendix of the Year 110 (2021) handbook ([Bookstart reading handbook](https://wwwacc.ntl.edu.tw/public/Attachment/16715141325.pdf)), rewritten in everyday language.

Age Child's characteristics Suitable books Shared reading tips
0–6 months Long sleep periods; blurry vision but can track movement; likes looking at faces; acute hearing and touch. Toy books with vivid colors, simple outlines, large patterns, and special shapes; cloth books with different textures that can be grasped and squeezed. Sing lullabies and nursery rhymes while caring for the baby; hold and talk to the baby often; place pictures or toys with strong color contrast near the sleeping area.

6–12 months Gradually able to sit; starting to crawl; likes grabbing things and will try to take and turn pages; puts things in their mouth; notices patterns in books and pats them; can distinguish different speech sounds. Cloth books and bath books; picture books with short words and simple patterns; sturdy, easy-to-turn board books; interactive play books. Use vocal variation or small sound-making props to play story games together; let the child freely touch books and guide them to learn page-turning; point to illustrations and name them during shared reading.

1–2 years Starting to learn to talk; can stand and walk; short attention span, easily distracted; can hold books and turn pages forward and back. Picture books related to daily experience (food, toys); picture books with vivid colors, large illustrations, and few words; play books. During bath or hygiene routines, chant body-part songs with matching actions; let the child be in charge of turning pages, or use a playful approach to tell the story with varied vocal expressions and body language.

2–3 years More vocabulary and sentence patterns; loves asking "what's that?"; beginning to understand simple cause and effect; will repeatedly read the same book. Picture books with simple plots and repetitive sentence patterns; content based on the child's daily routines and habits, such as eating, bathing, brushing teeth, using the toilet, sleeping, and visiting the doctor. Slow down when telling the story; pay attention to whether sentence length is easy for the child to remember and imitate.

3–5 years Strong imitation; rich imagination; simple logical reasoning; fluent verbal expression. Books with humorous and interesting plots; books about emotions; life stories that broaden experience; stories about family affection and friendship; informational picture books. Guide the child to recognize the correspondence between characters and sounds; when discussing the story, adults share their own experiences and thoughts; encourage the child to tell stories to family members.

## 2. 3 things to remember

1. Age is a reference, not a threshold.  The table shows common characteristics for each stage; the child's interest and state today are more accurate than the age column.

2. Shared reading can continue after age 5.  The American Academy of Pediatrics' 2024 policy statement recommends that shared reading begin at birth and continue at least through kindergarten. ([Pediatrics 2024](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39342414/)) The source handbook covers ages 0–5, so stages after age 5 are not listed in this article.

3. Choose books that the adults themselves find interesting.  The handbook's shared reading FAQ notes that if even the adult finds it boring, it's hard to muster the energy to read it to the child.

# How Can I Help My Child Practice Speaking at Home? Back-and-Forth Talk Matters More Than Saying More | Q&A Library | Think BIG

[← Q&A Library](https://thinkbigtw.com/en/qa/)

熊好學 · BearSay Mandarin BS03

# How Can I Help My Child Practice Speaking at Home? Back-and-Forth Talk Matters More Than Saying More

Think BIG Q&A Library　·　November 9, 2026 　·　[中文版](https://thinkbigtw.com/library/qa/practice-speaking-at-home/)

Short answer

Practising speaking at home works best as back-and-forth talk, not as a one-way flow of more sentences. Romeo and colleagues (2018) recorded the home language of 36 children aged 4 to 6 and scanned their brains while they listened to stories. Children who had more conversational turns with adults showed stronger activity in language-related brain regions, and this link held after accounting for socioeconomic status, IQ and the number of words adults spoke to the child. It is a small correlational study and cannot prove cause, so it is best read as a reason to try back-and-forth conversation, not as proof that it works.

## 1. What the study did

Romeo and colleagues (2018) used home audio recordings to count, for 36 children aged 4 to 6, the number of conversational turns with adults and the amount of adult speech directed to the child. The children then listened to stories during functional MRI. Children with more conversational turns showed greater activation in the left inferior frontal region (Broca's area), and this activation helped explain the link between language experience and verbal skill. ([Psychological Science, 2018](https://doi.org/10.1177/0956797617742725))

Item Detail
Participants 36 children aged 4 to 6 from varied family backgrounds

Measures Home recordings (conversational turns, adult speech); brain activity while listening to stories

Finding More conversational turns, stronger language-region activity, independent of socioeconomic status, IQ and adult speech quantity

## 2. Limits

Correlation, not cause.  The study did not ask one group of families to talk more and compare outcomes, so it cannot show that more conversation makes the brain response stronger.

Small sample.  36 children, and the study did not look at a Mandarin-learning setting.

No target amount.  It does not say how many turns a day are needed.

## 3. Five ways to practise speaking at home

1. Ask open questions.  Ask "What do you think?" or "Why?" more than yes-or-no questions. When the child answers in their own words, they are practising speaking.

2. Wait for the child to finish.  Pause for a few seconds after asking, and do not speak for the child while they are still thinking.

3. Expand the child's words a little.  If the child says "car," reply "Yes, a red car is coming," then pass the ball back: "Where is it going?"

4. Use daily routines.  Bath time, shopping and walking all work, with no special materials. For picture-book reading see [dialogic reading at home (Chinese)](https://thinkbigtw.com/library/qa/dialogic-reading-at-home/).

5. Do not interrupt mistakes.  Let the child finish, then naturally say it back the correct way instead of correcting every sentence, so the child stays willing to speak.

Brand information | BearSay Mandarin

## Pairing BearSay Mandarin with talk at home

BearSay Mandarin (熊好學) is a learning brand for Taiwan Mandarin. Every day it teaches one Taiwan Mandarin word on Instagram ([@bearsaymandarin](https://www.instagram.com/bearsaymandarin/)), in Traditional characters with zhuyin and pinyin and multilingual subtitles, guided by five characters: BUBU, MIBO, HUBO, GUIBO and LANBO. The app is in development and has not been released. Release information will appear on the [BearSay Mandarin Q&A overview](https://thinkbigtw.com/en/qa/bearsay/).

The daily word can start a conversation: after watching it, ask the child to say a sentence with that word, then keep asking follow-up questions. Speaking practice still depends on real two-way conversation.

Source: the public Instagram account and this site's brand overview, updated 2026-11-09. Demo audio is AI-synthesized speech; BearSay Mandarin characters are AI-generated.

## Frequently asked questions

Q1: How can I help my child practice speaking at home? Make it back-and-forth: ask open questions, wait for the child to finish, expand their words a little, use daily routines, and say mistakes back correctly instead of correcting every sentence. Q2: Do conversational turns really make a difference? Romeo and colleagues (2018) studied 36 children aged 4 to 6 and found that more conversational turns with adults were linked to stronger language-related brain responses, independent of socioeconomic status, IQ and adult speech quantity. It is correlational and does not prove cause. Q3: Is talking more or talking together more important? In that study, the link with conversational turns held after accounting for how much adults spoke, which suggests the back-and-forth itself has an independent association. Q4: Should I correct my child's mistakes right away? Not necessarily. Letting the child finish and then saying it back correctly is a common approach that reduces the chance the child stops speaking. It is practical advice, not a conclusion of that study.

Sources (links checked 2026-11-09)

- Romeo, Leonard, Robinson, West, Mackey, Rowe & Gabrieli (2018). Beyond the 30-million-word gap: Children's conversational exposure is associated with language-related brain function. Psychological Science, 29(5), 700–710: [doi.org](https://doi.org/10.1177/0956797617742725)

# Prompt Injection in AI Agents: Risks & Defences | Think BIG

[← Q&A Library](https://thinkbigtw.com/en/qa/)

Enterprise AI Security
TB04

# What Is Prompt Injection, and Can Documents or Web Pages an AI Agent Reads Give It Instructions?

Think BIG Q&A Library  ·  2026-10-19
      ·  [中文](https://thinkbigtw.com/library/qa/prompt-injection-ai-agent/)

The short answer

Yes. Prompt injection hides instructions in content the AI will read so that it does something it should not. When the instructions sit in outside content such as web pages, documents, or résumés, it is called indirect prompt injection. OWASP lists it as LLM01 in its 2025 Top 10 for large language model applications and states it is unclear whether fool-proof prevention exists. So the goal for a company is that even if the AI is fooled, it cannot do anything dangerous.

## 1. How prompt injection happens

OWASP's definition: a prompt injection occurs when input alters the model's behavior or output in unintended ways. There are two kinds:

- Direct prompt injection : the user types input meant to make the AI break its rules.

- Indirect prompt injection : the AI takes in content from an outside source (a website or file) that contains hidden instructions, and treats them as commands. These can be invisible to people, such as white text on a white background.

OWASP's scenarios include: an AI asked to summarize a web page whose hidden instructions cause it to leak the private conversation; a résumé uploaded with malicious instructions split across sections, which manipulate the model's evaluation of the candidate; and an attacker modifying a document in a RAG knowledge base to change the AI's answers.

Why AI Agents need more care than chat AI:  a fooled chatbot says something wrong; a fooled AI Agent that can send email, query data, or edit files may actually act.

How it differs from jailbreaking:  Jailbreaking is a form of prompt injection aimed at making the model ignore its safety rules; prompt injection is broader and covers any input that alters the model's behavior. OWASP notes the terms are often used interchangeably.

## 2. Five defenses a company can put in place

OWASP's recommendations, in a form companies can apply:

- Separate outside content from instructions.  Web pages, emails, and attachments the AI reads are marked as data, not instructions. The system prompt states the AI's role and limits.

- Least privilege.  An AI Agent that reads outside email does not get permission to send email or delete files. Sensitive functions are handled in code, not left to the model.

- Human approval for high-risk actions.  Sending externally, spending money, deleting, or changing production data happens only after a person confirms. Even if the AI is fooled, it stops at that gate.

- Check output formats in code.  Define the expected output format and validate it with deterministic code; anything that does not match is blocked.

- Run adversarial tests regularly.  Treat the model as an untrusted user and test whether trust boundaries hold.

OWASP also notes that RAG and fine-tuning make answers more relevant and accurate, but research shows they do not fully mitigate prompt injection. The defenses have to come from permissions and process, not the model alone.

## 3. A quick self-check

Ask your provider or your IT team:

- Which content written by others does this AI Agent read? (Web pages, customer emails, uploaded files, shared documents)

- After reading it, what actions can it take? (Send email, change data, pay, call external services)

- Which actions always pause for a person to confirm?

Anything that both reads outside content and can act directly, with no human check in between, is the first thing to fix.

Brand information | Think BIG

## FAQ

Q1: What is indirect prompt injection? The AI takes in content from an outside source such as a web page or file, and hidden instructions in that content get treated as commands. The instructions may be invisible to people. Q2: How is prompt injection different from jailbreaking? OWASP notes the terms are often used interchangeably. The goal is that a fooled AI still cannot do anything dangerous.

# RAG Access Control by Department: How-To Guide | Think BIG

[← Q&A Library](https://thinkbigtw.com/en/qa/)

Building AI Agents
TB10

# When AI Searches Company Documents, How Do You Make Sure Each Department Sees Only Its Own Data?

Think BIG Q&A Library  ·  2026-10-19
      ·  [中文](https://thinkbigtw.com/library/qa/rag-access-control-by-department/)

The short answer

Enforce permissions at the retrieval step, not by relying on the AI's judgment. When indexing, tag each document with its department and the roles allowed to read it. When an employee asks a question, the system searches only documents that person may see, so restricted passages never reach the AI. Then verify with test questions for content the user must not see, confirming neither the answer nor the citations expose it.

## 1. Why "don't reveal this" in the prompt is not enough

In retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), the system first finds relevant passages and then hands them to the model to write the answer. Once a restricted passage is retrieved and placed in the model's context, the model has seen it. Asking it through the prompt not to repeat it is unreliable: the model can make mistakes or be steered by prompt injection.

OWASP's 2025 Top 10 for LLM Applications lists this as LLM08, Vector and Embedding Weaknesses: inadequate or misaligned access controls can allow unauthorized access to embeddings containing sensitive information, and when multiple classes of users share one vector database, context can leak between users or queries. OWASP recommends fine-grained access controls with permission-aware vector and embedding stores, and strict logical and access partitioning of datasets.

## 2. Four steps

- Inventory documents and tag permissions.  Record each document's owner, current version, department, and allowed roles. Documents without permission tags stay out of the knowledge base.

- Store permissions with the index.  Each chunk carries the permission tags of its source document. Highly sensitive data, such as HR and payroll, can go into a separate knowledge base.

- Filter before retrieval.  Based on the person asking, search only the scope they may see. The system makes the authorization decision, not the model. OWASP LLM06 calls this complete mediation: enforce authorization in downstream systems instead of relying on the model.

- Verify with must-not-see tests.  For example, have a regular employee account ask about a rule only managers may see, and confirm neither the answer nor the citations expose it.

## 3. Three common gaps

Gap
How it happens
How to close it
Citations leak
The answer does not say it, but the attached source link or excerpt exposes restricted content
Apply the same permissions to citations

Permissions out of sync
An employee changes department or leaves; the file system is updated, but the knowledge base tags are not
Sync permissions from a single source and spot-check regularly

Withdrawn document still indexed
An old rule is withdrawn but its passages remain in the index, so the AI answers by the old rule
Update the index when withdrawing documents and log it as a change

## FAQ

Q1: Can an AI knowledge base have department-level permissions? Yes. Tag each passage with department and allowed roles when indexing, and search only the scope the asker may see, so restricted passages never reach the AI. Q2: Is telling the AI in the prompt not to reveal secrets enough? No. Once a restricted passage is retrieved into the context, the model has seen it and may reveal it by mistake or under prompt injection. The system must block it at retrieval. Q3: Is it safe for several departments to share one vector database? Only with access control. # RAG Data Flow: Cloud vs. On-Premises Comparison | Think BIG

[← Q&A Library](https://thinkbigtw.com/en/qa/)

Enterprise AI Security
TB03

# When AI Searches Company Documents, Where Does the Data Go in Cloud vs. On-Premises Setups?

Think BIG Q&A Library  ·  2026-10-19
      ·  [中文](https://thinkbigtw.com/library/qa/rag-data-flow-cloud-vs-local/)

The short answer

On-premises: employees' questions, company documents, and the AI's answers are all processed on the company's own hardware. Cloud-assisted: the employee's question, plus the document passages the system retrieves, are sent to the model provider and retained for a period under the provider's rules (for example, up to 30 days by default for the OpenAI and Anthropic APIs). One more check: if the embedding step used for indexing also runs on a cloud service, document content is sent out in chunks when the index is built.

## 1. The four stages data passes through

The common way to let AI search company documents is RAG (retrieval-augmented generation): before answering, the AI retrieves relevant passages from company documents and writes the answer from them. The approach comes from Lewis et al. (2020). Data passes four stages:

Stage
What happens
On-premises
Cloud-assisted
1. Indexing
Documents are split and converted to vectors in a knowledge base
On company hardware
Depends: a local embedding model keeps it in-house; a cloud embedding API sends the passages out

2. Retrieval
Relevant passages are found for the question
On company hardware
Usually on company hardware or a server under the company's account

3. Answering
"Question + retrieved passages" go to the model
Model on company hardware
Question and passages go to the model provider

4. Logging
Chat logs, system logs, backups
Stored where the company designates
The company keeps its own logs; the provider retains data under its own policy

Stage 3 is the key. The cloud-assisted version does not send the whole knowledge base, but every question sends the passages retrieved for it. More questions mean more document fragments leave the company.

## 2. How long providers retain data

Per official documentation (checked 2026-10-19):

- OpenAI API : since March 1, 2023, API data is not used for training by default. Abuse monitoring logs, which may include prompts and responses, are retained up to 30 days by default. Eligible customers can apply for Zero Data Retention, subject to OpenAI's prior approval.

- Anthropic API : inputs and outputs are deleted within 30 days of receipt or generation by default. Exceptions include customer-controlled storage (such as the Files API), separate agreements, Usage Policy enforcement, and legal requirements.

So the cloud-assisted version means two things: data leaves the company, and it stays on someone else's servers for a while. If a policy says a document must never leave the company, it belongs only in the on-premises knowledge base.

## 3. Five questions to ask before you start

- Where does embedding happen?  A local model or a cloud API? With a cloud API, document content leaves when the index is built.

- Where is the answering model?  Local or a cloud provider? Under whose account?

- Where are chat logs and system logs kept, and for how long?  Who can see them?

- What other external services are connected?  LINE, email, cloud storage: messages through any of these pass through that service.

- Which documents must never leave?  List them and confirm they only go into the on-premises knowledge base.

If all five have clear answers, the data flow is understood. Any question without an answer is where to dig further.

# How Much Screen Time Is Right for Under-5s? What Role Can Printed Books Play at Home | Think BIG Q&A Library

[← Q&A Library](https://thinkbigtw.com/en/qa/)

Shared Reading & Custom Picture Books
Q20

# How Much Screen Time Is Right for Under-5s? What Role Can Printed Books Play at Home

Think BIG Q&A Library  ·  2026-10-30
      ·  [中文](https://thinkbigtw.com/library/qa/screen-time-under-5/)

The short answer

The World Health Organization's (WHO) 2019 guidelines recommend: no screen time for children under 1; no prolonged sedentary screen time for 1-year-olds; no more than 1 hour of sedentary screen time per day for children aged 2–4, and less is better. When children are seated, caregivers are encouraged to read and tell stories with them. The Health Promotion Administration's (NHA) 2014 guidelines on 3C product vision care state: no screen time for children under 2; no more than 1 hour per day for children aged 2 and over; take a 10-minute break after every 30 minutes of use. Physical books can be placed in time slots that were previously used for screen time, as a quiet activity done with an adult present.

## 1. What the two sets of guidelines say

Age World Health Organization (2019) Health Promotion Administration (2014 — 3C product vision care notice)
Under 1 Screen time not recommended; when seated, caregivers are encouraged to read and tell stories with the child. No screen time for children under 2.

1 year Prolonged sedentary screen time not recommended (e.g., watching TV, videos, playing computer games); when seated, caregivers are encouraged to read and tell stories with the child. No screen time for children under 2.

2 years No more than 1 hour of sedentary screen time per day, and less is better; when seated, caregivers are encouraged to read and tell stories with the child. No more than 1 hour of screen time per day for children aged 2 and over; take a 10-minute break after every 30 minutes of use.

3–4 years No more than 1 hour of sedentary screen time per day, and less is better; when seated, caregivers are encouraged to read and tell stories with the child. No more than 1 hour of screen time per day for children aged 2 and over; take a 10-minute break after every 30 minutes of use.

WHO's recommendation comes from Guidelines on physical activity, sedentary behaviour and sleep for children under 5 years of age , published on 24 April 2019; the press release also notes that non-screen interactive activities done with a caregiver — such as reading, storytelling, singing, and puzzles — are very important for children's development. ([WHO press release](https://www.who.int/news/item/24-04-2019-to-grow-up-healthy-children-need-to-sit-less-and-play-more), [WHO guidelines page](https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789241550536))

The NHA's recommendation came from the notice on precautions for 3C product vision care established at a government-academic industry meeting on 5 June 2014. ([Ministry of Health and Welfare website, source: Health Promotion Administration](https://mohw.gov.tw/cp-16-21201-1.html))

## 2. Where physical books fit in

Both sets of guidelines focus on "less screen time"; WHO additionally names reading and storytelling as activities to do together with a caregiver. The following are practical suggestions, not content from the above sources:

1. First identify the most common screen-time slot.  For example, after dinner or when adults are doing chores. Start by changing just one slot — no need to change everything at once.

2. Replace it with an adult reading alongside.  WHO specifies reading and storytelling done "with a caregiver" — giving a child a book to look at alone is different from an adult reading with them.

3. Keep books in a place the child can reach.  Put away the tablet and place books at a height the child can grab.

4. Switch to reading before bed.  For how to structure the bedtime routine, see [How to start bedtime shared reading](https://thinkbigtw.com/en/qa/bedtime-reading-routine/).

## 3. What if it's hard to do

WHO's phrasing is "less is better," not "failure if you go over." Starting with a little less than yesterday is enough; an adult staying present during screen time, and chatting about the content afterward, are both better than leaving the child to watch alone. For what books suit each age, see [What picture books suit each stage from ages 0–5?](https://thinkbigtw.com/en/qa/picture-books-by-age/)

WHO's 2019 guidelines do not recommend screen time for children under 1, and do not recommend prolonged sedentary screen time for 1-year-olds; the NHA's 2014 3C product vision care notice states no screen time for children under 2. Q2: How much screen time can a 3–4-year-old have per day? # Is It Safe to Post Children's Photos Online? 4 Things to Consider Before You Share | Think BIG Q&A Library

[← Q&A Library](https://thinkbigtw.com/en/qa/)

Shared Reading & Custom Picture Books
Q28

# Is It Safe to Post Children's Photos Online? 4 Things to Consider Before You Share

Think BIG Q&A Library  ·  2026-11-07
      ·  [中文](https://thinkbigtw.com/library/qa/sharing-kids-photos-online/)

The short answer

Before deciding whether to post a child's photos online, it is recommended to first consider whether the child is willing, who can see them, what information the image reveals, and how to handle deletion later — then decide whether to share. UNICEF notes that online sharing cannot be entirely risk-free; parents can choose photo by photo and do not need to make everything public. The following are family privacy suggestions for reference and do not constitute legal advice.

## 1. First distinguish between keeping photos, sharing with family, and sharing publicly

Keeping photos at home, sharing them in a family group chat, and posting them on a public page are three different arrangements. [UNICEF's sharenting page](https://www.unicef.org/parenting/child-care/sharenting) includes video sharing on messaging platforms in its discussion, not just public social media. So the next time you want to share a photo, you can first ask "who do I actually want to see this?" before deciding where to post it.

When a child is old enough to express their wishes, it is recommended to show them the selected photo and explain who it will be shared with; if they say they don't want it shared, choose a different one or don't share. For young children who cannot yet understand the consequences of sharing, UNICEF notes they cannot give informed consent, and parents still need to consider their privacy and feelings on their behalf. This should not be simplified to "the child nodded, so any use is fine."

## 2. Ask yourself these 4 questions before pressing send

What to consider Check you can do at home How will the child see this in the future? Start by not sharing images of nudity, embarrassment, uncontrolled crying, or private caregiving; when in doubt, keep it for yourself.

Who is actually the audience? Check the account visibility settings, group members, and album permissions once — not just relying on the impression that "this is a private account."

What information does it reveal? Check for name tags, school badges, addresses, schedule text, and other people's faces; unnecessary information can be cropped out or omitted.

What if you change your mind? Confirm whether you can delete the post and how to ask family members to remove it; agree with family in advance to ask before forwarding.

This checklist is organized based on UNICEF's reminders about audience, identifiable information, embarrassing images, and communication with family and friends; it is not a test where passing all four items eliminates risk. You can also first share a photo of a craft the child made without showing their face, saying only what you did together that day — putting the emphasis on the experience rather than the image.

## 3. Even if you've already shared, you can adjust starting today

You can start by reviewing recent albums, selecting content that no longer needs to be public, and deleting or adjusting visibility photo by photo; then tell family members "please ask us before forwarding photos of the children in the future." This is a sample family agreement — it doesn't require sorting through all old photos at once, nor does it place all responsibility on one caregiver.

If you are submitting photos to a provider to make a book, see the separate collection notification. The Personal Data Protection Act Article 8 covers the period, territory, recipients, and methods of data use; Article 3 covers rights to inquire, correct, stop use, and request deletion. ([Laws and Regulations Database](https://law.moj.gov.tw/LawClass/LawAll.aspx?pcode=I0050021)) Submitting to a production service and sharing publicly are different uses and cannot be equated.

For specific questions, see [privacy questions before making a custom book](https://thinkbigtw.com/en/qa/photo-privacy-custom-book/); if what you're sharing includes photos of both adults and children, you can also refer to [consent and handling of adults' photos](https://thinkbigtw.com/en/qa/parents-in-custom-book/).

When family members disagree, it is also fine to hold off on posting and discuss the specific photo together first.

Even private sharing requires considering the child's feelings and identifiable information. Q2: If the child says they don't want a photo shared publicly, what should I do? Their wishes can be respected — keep it for yourself or choose different content; there is no need to make sharing a condition of their cooperation in taking photos. Q3: If I've shared a lot of photos before, can I sort through them now? You can start by reviewing recent content, deleting posts you no longer need to keep public, then discuss future sharing practices with family members. # How to Talk to Children About Taiwan's Festivals: Shared-Reading Approaches for 7 Holidays | Think BIG Q&A Library

[← Q&A Library](https://thinkbigtw.com/en/qa/)

Shared Reading & Custom Picture Books
Q19

# How to Talk to Children About Taiwan's Festivals: Shared-Reading Approaches for 7 Holidays

Think BIG Q&A Library  ·  2026-10-29
      ·  [中文](https://thinkbigtw.com/library/qa/taiwan-festivals-for-kids/)

The short answer

When talking about festivals with children, starting with "how does our family celebrate" is the easiest approach: first ask what the child remembers, then look at the calendar to find the date, and finally talk about the festival's origins and customs. For dates, the Commemorative Days and Holidays Implementation Regulations can be consulted: Chinese New Year (Spring Festival), Lantern Festival, Qingming, Dragon Boat Festival, Mid-Autumn Festival, and New Year's Eve are all listed as folk holidays; National Day is a commemorative day. Among these, New Year's Eve and Spring Festival have 5 days off; Qingming, Dragon Boat Festival, and Mid-Autumn Festival each have 1 day off; National Day has 1 day off; the Lantern Festival has no holiday; and the Winter Solstice is not listed among the holidays in the Regulations.

## 1. 7 festivals — what the regulations say

The Commemorative Days and Holidays Implementation Regulations, promulgated and implemented on 28 May 2025, list commemorative days in Article 3, folk holidays in Article 5, and holidays in Articles 4 and 6 ([Laws and Regulations Database](https://law.moj.gov.tw/LawClass/LawAll.aspx?pcode=D0020095)):

Festival Date in the Regulations Is it a holiday?
New Year's Eve Last day of the 12th lunar month (folk holiday) New Year's Eve and Spring Festival: from the day before New Year's Eve through the 3rd day of the 1st lunar month — 5 days off

Lantern Festival 15th day of the 1st lunar month (folk holiday) No holiday

Qingming Festival Set to the Qingming solar term (folk holiday) 1 day off; separate rules apply when it falls on the same day as Children's Day

Dragon Boat Festival 5th day of the 5th lunar month (folk holiday) 1 day off

Mid-Autumn Festival 15th day of the 8th lunar month (folk holiday) 1 day off

National Day October 10 (commemorative day) 1 day off

Winter Solstice Not listed in the Regulations —

When a holiday falls on a day off, a makeup day is provided (Article 8). Article 5 of the Regulations also lists Ghost Festival (Zhongyuan), Double Ninth Festival (Chongyang), and Indigenous People's harvest festivals as folk holidays; Article 3 also includes National Hakka Day (December 28). Taiwan has more than these 7 festivals; how your family celebrates is something to choose from your own customs.

## 2. How the curriculum framework views festivals

The Ministry of Education's Preschool Curriculum Framework lists "people and the environment" as a learning dimension in the social domain, with content including understanding the various roles and activities of people in the community, cultural customs and festivals, and diverse ways of living; the curriculum objectives also include "understanding cultural diversity in the living environment." ([Ministry of Education Legal System](https://edu.law.moe.gov.tw/LawContent.aspx?id=GL001586)) For children, festivals are a window into understanding "how other families and our family celebrate."

## 3. 4 ways to talk about festivals

The following are practical suggestions, not content from the regulations or curriculum framework:

1. Start by asking what the child remembers.  "Last Chinese New Year, whose house did we go to? What did we eat?" Starting from the child's own experience is easier to connect with than explaining origins first.

2. Look at the calendar together and find the date.  The folk holidays in the Regulations mostly use the lunar calendar; National Day uses the solar calendar. Circle them on the calendar — the child will discover that some holidays fall on different solar calendar dates each year.

3. Start with what to eat and what to do.  For each festival, pick one thing the child can experience: what to eat, what to do, where to go — these are easier to remember than reciting origins.

4. Let the child tell "how our family celebrates."  Every family celebrates the same festival differently; encourage the child to tell family members or classmates — this is what the curriculum framework means by understanding cultural diversity.

For Taiwan's geography and places, see [Is there a Taiwan-themed picture book where the child is the main character?](https://thinkbigtw.com/en/qa/taiwan-themed-picture-book/) This article covers only festivals.

## FAQ

Q1: What are Taiwan's folk holidays? Under Article 5 of the Commemorative Days and Holidays Implementation Regulations, the folk holidays are: Spring Festival, Lantern Festival, Qingming Festival, Dragon Boat Festival, Ghost Festival (Zhongyuan), Mid-Autumn Festival, Double Ninth Festival (Chongyang), New Year's Eve, and Indigenous People's harvest festivals. Q2: Is the Lantern Festival a public holiday? No. Article 6 of the Commemorative Days and Holidays Implementation Regulations specifies the holidays with time off — New Year's Eve and Spring Festival (5 days), Children's Day, Qingming Festival, Labor Day, Dragon Boat Festival, Teachers' Day, Mid-Autumn Festival (1 day each), and so on; the Lantern Festival is not among them. Q3: Is the Winter Solstice an official holiday? Neither Article 3's commemorative days nor Article 5's folk holidays in the Commemorative Days and Holidays Implementation Regulations list the Winter Solstice, so it is not a holiday under the Regulations and there is no day off. Q4: Is there a custom picture book about Taiwan's festivals with the child as the main character? Yes. Tale With You's "Taiwan Festivals" theme is [Child's name]'s Year of Festivals — from New Year's Eve reunion dinner to Winter Solstice tangyuan, with the main character illustrated based on the child's photos. # Is There a Taiwan-Themed Picture Book Starring Your Child? Using One Book to Explore Taiwan | Think BIG Q&A Library

Shared Reading & Custom Picture Books
Q04

# Is There a Taiwan-Themed Picture Book Starring Your Child? Using One Book to Explore Taiwan

Think BIG Q&A Library  ·  2026-10-14
      ·  [中文](https://thinkbigtw.com/library/qa/taiwan-themed-picture-book/)

The short answer

Yes. Custom picture books where the child is the main character already include Taiwan-themed options — for example, Tale With You's "Taiwan Island Tour" places the child (in their own likeness) in book pages featuring Taipei, Keelung, Jiufen, Hualien, Kenting, Alishan, and Penghu; the "Taiwan Festivals" theme follows a year of festivals. To help children truly remember these places, the most effective approach is to connect the book pages with maps and real outings.

## 1. Why put the child "in" Taiwan's scenery

Children engage more with content that relates to themselves. Research has found that 3-year-old children learn new words faster in book passages where they are the main character (see [Do books where the child is the main character really help with reading?](https://thinkbigtw.com/en/qa/personalized-book-research/)). Place names, vehicles, and local specialties placed in the context of "I took the train to Hualien" are easier to remember than on a list in a textbook.

Taiwan-themed books have another advantage: the places in the book might be somewhere you can actually visit the next weekend. When the book and the real world connect, the child will keep coming back to it.

## 2. An "island-tour reading map" you can make at home

1. Get a map of Taiwan.  A large one or an A4 printout works. Each time you read about a stop, let the child place a small sticker on the map.

2. Ask only one question per stop.  "How do we get to Penghu?" (by boat), "What do we take to get to Jiufen?" — no need to explain a lot at once; one question per stop is enough.

3. Add one real fact per stop.  Use publicly available government information as your material, so when the child asks "really?" you can answer. For example:

- Kenting:  Established in Year 71 of the Republic of China (1982), it is Taiwan's first national park; its management office was established in Year 73. Other national parks including Yushan, Yangmingshan, and Taroko followed. ([Executive Yuan national profile](https://www.ey.gov.tw/state/4447F4A951A1EC45/dc08391a-c57c-4cf7-af9a-cc0d9e4ebb1c))

- Alishan:  The Alishan Forest Railway was out of service for many years following Typhoon Morakot; after 15 years, it restored full-line service on 6 July 2024; Alishan Station sits at an elevation of 2,216 meters. ([Forestry and Nature Conservation Agency, Ministry of Agriculture](https://www.forest.gov.tw/MagazineFile/7277))

4. Bring the book on real outings.  When you reach a place that has appeared in the book, find an angle similar to the book page and take a photo. Back home, place the photo next to the book — the child will feel a great sense of achievement.

## 3. From geography to festivals

Knowing Taiwan means not just "where to go" but also "how people live." New Year's Eve reunion dinner, Lantern Festival parade, Dragon Boat Festival race, Mid-Autumn Festival moon-gazing — these festivals come around every year, and reading about them in the week before each one, then actually celebrating them, makes the connection complete.

# My Child Loves Vehicles: 4 Ways to Turn That Interest Into an Observation Activity | Think BIG Q&A Library

[← Q&A Library](https://thinkbigtw.com/en/qa/)

Shared Reading & Custom Picture Books
Q23

# My Child Loves Vehicles: 4 Ways to Turn That Interest Into an Observation Activity

Think BIG Q&A Library  ·  2026-11-02
      ·  [中文](https://thinkbigtw.com/library/qa/vehicles-loving-kids/)

The short answer

When a child loves vehicles, you can start with 4 activities — finding details, comparing uses, drawing routes, and telling stories — turning watching vehicles into shared observation time. First connect with the specific vehicle the child likes, then ask one easy question; there's no need to rush into naming every vehicle. The following are family activity suggestions; there's no requirement to complete everything each time, and they don't treat the results as an ability test.

## 1. First follow the interest when choosing books; don't rush to quiz on knowledge

The American Academy of Pediatrics' [read-aloud recommendations](https://www.healthychildren.org/English/ages-stages/gradeschool/school/Pages/Help-Your-Child-Enjoy-Reading-Aloud-Tips-for-Parents.aspx) note that book selection can follow the child's interests, and there's no need to push through the story when the child loses interest. For a vehicle-loving child, shared reading can start with one familiar vehicle image, letting the child point and say something before deciding whether to keep flipping.

For example, if the child only wants to look at the excavator, start by looking at that page together. You can say "you're looking at its long arm," then ask "what do you think it's about to dig?" If the child only gives a one-word reply, pick up that word; if they give no reply, the adult can share their own observation instead. The question here is an example, not a standard the child should reach.

## 2. Try these 4 activities at home

Activity How to do it Things you can say Find details Pick one image and take turns finding doors, windows, or wheels, then point them out to each other. "I found a door — what did you find?"

Compare uses Put two vehicle images side by side and think about what each would carry or do. "If we needed to move a lot of dirt, which one would you call?"

Draw a route Draw home, the train station, and the park on paper, then run a toy vehicle along the road. "Starting from home, where do you want to go first?"

Tell a story Draw a vehicle the child saw today; the child gives it a name, and the adult writes one sentence. "What happened to this vehicle today?"

Pick just one activity at a time. Without a toy vehicle, a finger can walk the route; without drawing, use books at home as stations. If the child reimagines it as a flying bus, go along with the story. If you want to look up how a real vehicle works, write the question down and find a reliable source later — no need to guess on the spot.

## 3. Bring observations back into daily life, and keep them in the book

When going out to look at vehicles, it's recommended to choose a stable, traffic-separated position and have an adult present; stay only where it's safe to stay and don't step into traffic areas for a photo. Back home, flip to a similar page and ask "how was what we saw just now different from the book?" This is an outing planning suggestion — no need to make a special long trip.

The AAP's [reading in family life recommendations](https://www.healthychildren.org/English/ages-stages/gradeschool/school/Pages/10-Tips-to-Help-Your-Child-Fall-in-Love-with-Reading.aspx) also encourage parents to read what their child is reading. Adults can pick a vehicle book together and share their own favorite page; for details neither of you knows, look them up together. When you want to switch topics next time, the same activities can transition to [dinosaur-themed shared reading extensions](https://thinkbigtw.com/en/qa/dinosaur-loving-kids/); for ideas on how to ask questions, see [dialogic shared reading](https://thinkbigtw.com/en/qa/dialogic-reading-at-home/).

If the child asks about the same vehicle many times, write the question on paper and bring it out the next time you read. Parents can also take turns being the asker, letting the child ask "what do you see?" and hearing what each notices. It's suggested to keep this paper as a conversation record — no ranking, no timing, no requirement for a new discovery each time; if today you just laughed and flipped through a few pages together, that is also a fine place to stop.

The theme has Style A (watercolor album) and Style B (toy-figure 3D); both styles use the same story, and one is chosen at the time of ordering. The sample page's featured character is an AI-generated image; the actual illustration is generated from the submitted photo and may differ from the person's appearance; a preview will be provided for confirmation before printing.

## FAQ

Q1: If the child only wants to read vehicle books, should we switch? You can first read the content they like, then invite them to choose other topics — no need to force a change each time. Q2: If the child can't yet name vehicles, how can we do shared reading together? The child can point to illustrations, imitate sounds, or the adult can describe the image; there's no need to already know vehicle names before you can do shared reading. Q3: Do observation activities require a lot of toys? No. One book, one piece of paper, and a finger are enough for finding details or drawing a route. Q4: Does Tale With You have a vehicles theme? Yes, titled [Child's name]'s Vehicle Roundup, available in both watercolor album and toy-figure 3D art styles.

# What Is an AI Agent, and How Does It Differ from a Chatbot? | Q&A Library | Think BIG

[← Q&A Library](https://thinkbigtw.com/en/qa/)

AI Basics
TB21

# What Is an AI Agent, and How Does It Differ from a Chatbot?

Think BIG Q&A Library  ·  2026-11-03
      ·  [中文](https://thinkbigtw.com/library/qa/what-is-ai-agent/)

The short answer

An AI Agent uses a model to choose next steps, call tools, and continue based on the results. A chatbot usually centers on conversation, but a chat interface can also front an Agent. For a company, the useful distinction is what the system can read, what it can change, and when a person must approve an action.

## 1. Look at how work proceeds

Anthropic’s “Building effective agents” distinguishes predefined workflows from Agents that dynamically direct their processes and tool use. This is an architectural distinction, not a naming rule used by every vendor. A product labeled “Agent” still needs a clear account of its capabilities.

Approach
Illustrative meeting task
What to check
Conversation
Summarize the notes supplied by a person
Input permissions and accuracy

Fixed workflow
Read, summarize, and save in a predefined sequence
Inputs and error handling at each step

Agent
Choose tools and decide what to do after inspecting results
Tool access, stopping rules, and approvals

Actual file access, writing, and scheduling depend on implementation and authorization. A fluent response is insufficient evidence of completion; inspect the draft, tool result, or system record.

## 2. Separate suggestions from actions

OWASP LLM06:2025 identifies excessive functionality, permissions, and autonomy as causes of excessive agency. A document reader that also exposes deletion expands the possible harm. OWASP recommends narrower tools and permissions, plus human approval for high-impact actions.

Our suggested starting point is to distinguish lookup, drafting, writing, and external sending. Preparing a task list and updating a production system require different authorizations. Begin with approved read-only material and drafts; add actions after naming an approver, defining scope, and planning error handling. These are deployment recommendations, not features every Agent includes.

## 3. Define one task you can inspect

A useful brief could be: “Read approved files in this folder, draft this week’s tasks with supporting references, save the draft, and do not send it.” Test missing information, failed tools, and denied access as well as normal input. Check whether the system stops and explains the issue. Evaluate the work product as a whole.

Local versus cloud inference is a separate decision. Think BIG’s published guidance distinguishes deployment location from external connections: software on company hardware may still send data to cloud models or messaging services. Document data boundaries and action approvals before building.

Brand information | Think BIG

## Data and action boundaries for Think BIG AI Agents

Think BIG helps companies deploy AI Agents in their own environments. Running on company hardware does not keep every connection local: cloud models, messaging platforms, and other external services can still receive requests.

- Map data flows first : Before deployment, identify data sources, processing locations, output recipients, logs, and backups. Assess deployment location and external connections separately.

- Set permissions for the task : Define read and write access using least privilege. A designated person decides on external sending, spending, and changes to production systems.

See [Trust](https://thinkbigtw.com/trust/) and [Local AI and data sovereignty](https://thinkbigtw.com/guides/local-ai-data/).

The actual scope of Think BIG’s services follows what both parties confirm.

## FAQ

Q1: Does a chat interface mean it is just a chatbot? No. The interface does not reveal whether the system also calls tools or performs actions. Q2: Does every task need an Agent? No. Anthropic recommends starting with the simplest approach that meets the need, which may be a fixed workflow or a single model call. Q3: Can an Agent run on company hardware? Depending on its design, yes. Check models, tools, logs, and external connections separately. Q4: What access should a pilot receive? We suggest approved read-only sources and draft creation first, with human approval for high-impact actions.
